domains.name: The Terraform Language
domains.description: HCL mastery: resources, variables, expressions, and meta-arguments.

scenarios.title: The Unpinned Provider
scenarios.situation: A team's CI pipeline suddenly fails on `terraform init` — no config changed. The error: the AWS provider's newest major version renamed an argument their config uses. Their `required_providers` has no version constraint and the lock file is gitignored.
evidence: init pulled aws provider 6.x; argument renamed; no version constraint; lock gitignored.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the fix?
choices: Root cause: unpinned provider + ignored lock file let init resolve the newest major version with breaking schema changes. Fix: add `version = "~> 5.0"` (or their last-known-good major), delete the bad lock entries, re-init to regenerate `.terraform.lock.hcl`, commit the lock file, and remove it from .gitignore. The discipline: provider versions are dependencies — pinned and locked like any other.
Terraform is broken; downgrade the binary.
The config was wrong all along.
Delete the .terraform directory weekly.
scenarios.hint: CI breaks on init with no config change — provider renamed an argument. What is the cause and fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the exact mechanism (unconstrained version resolution pulling a breaking major) and gives the complete remediation (pin, regenerate lock, commit, un-ignore) plus the principle (providers are dependencies). B/C/D all miss the mechanism.

scenarios.title: The Plaintext Secret
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer marks the database password variable `sensitive = true` and concludes the secret is now secure. The state file is stored in a shared S3 bucket with broad read access.
evidence: db_password sensitive=true; state in S3 with broad read; engineer: 'secure.'
choices: `sensitive` is display hygiene only — the password is in the state file in plaintext, and the state also records it in plan logs and outputs. The broad S3 read access means the 'secured' secret is readable by anyone with bucket access. The fix: remote state with encryption + tight IAM, and ideally no long-lived secrets in config at all (use a secrets manager with dynamic credentials or Vault-injected values).
Sensitive variables encrypt the state.
S3 access doesn't matter for state.
The engineer did everything right.
scenarios.hint: A 'sensitive' DB password sits in broadly-readable state — what is wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It states precisely what sensitive does and doesn't do, identifies the actual exposure (plaintext in state + broad bucket access), and gives the layered fix (encrypted remote state, tight IAM, secrets manager). B/C/D all misunderstand the mechanism.

scenarios.title: The Renumbering Catastrophe
scenarios.situation: A team used `count` for 50 DNS records. They remove the first record from the list; Terraform plans to destroy and recreate all 49 remaining records (downtime, DNS churn).
evidence: remove list[0]; terraform wants to recreate all 49 remaining records.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix and the lesson?
choices: The lesson: count addresses by position — removing index 0 shifts every subsequent index, so Terraform sees 49 'new' identities. The fix: migrate to for_each keyed by record name (using moved blocks or state mv to preserve identities: `moved { from = aws_route53_record.r[0] to = aws_route53_record.r["www"] }`), so each record has a stable key. The rule: count for fungible replicas, for_each for anything with identity.
DNS records can't use for_each.
Recreate everything; it's fine.
Never remove records.
scenarios.hint: Removing one of 50 count-based DNS records recreates all 49 — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the positional-identity mechanism, gives the migration path (for_each + moved blocks preserving identity), and states the general rule. B is false; C/D surrender.

scenarios.title: The Detached Security Group
scenarios.situation: Replacing a security group caused a 2-minute outage: Terraform destroyed the old group first, detaching it from all instances, then created the new one. The team 'fixed' it by adding depends_on everywhere.
evidence: SG replacement: destroy-first, 2-min outage; 'fix': depends_on everywhere.
choices: `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` on the security group — the replacement ordering fix (new exists before old is destroyed). The depends_on carpet-bombing was the wrong tool: depends_on controls ORDER between resources, not the create/destroy sequencing of a single resource's replacement — and overuse obscures the real graph. The lesson: ordering problems need graph thinking (references, lifecycle), not depends_on sprinkles.
More depends_on will fix it.
Security groups can't be replaced safely.
Do replacements manually.
scenarios.hint: Security group replacement caused an outage; the team added depends_on everywhere — what is the correct fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes the two mechanisms precisely (create/destroy sequencing vs inter-resource ordering), gives the exact fix, and diagnoses the depends_on misuse. B doubles the error; C/D surrender.

scenarios.title: The Half-Provisioned Fleet
scenarios.situation: A team's remote-exec provisioner fails halfway through a 20-instance fleet (network blip). Ten instances are configured, ten aren't — and Terraform reports success because the resources (instances) created fine. Rerunning apply does nothing.
evidence: remote-exec failed on 10/20; terraform reports success; re-apply no-op.
choices: Provisioners execute outside the declarative model: Terraform tracked the instances (created ✓) but not the provisioner's effects — so the half-configured state is invisible to the graph, and apply won't converge it (provisioners run at create-time only). The lesson: configuration belongs in convergent systems (user_data re-runs on replacement; Ansible converges on every run) — anything Terraform can't see, it can't fix. The fleet needs Ansible/cloud-init, not provisioners.
Run apply again; it'll converge.
Provisioners need better networks.
Manually configure the ten.
scenarios.hint: A failed provisioner leaves half a fleet unconfigured; apply won't fix it — what is the lesson?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the invisibility mechanism (graph tracks resources, not provisioner effects; create-time-only execution), states the convergent-systems principle, and prescribes the replacement. B misunderstands; C/D treat symptoms.

scenarios.title: The Accidental Database
scenarios.situation: An engineer renames `aws_db_instance.main` to `aws_db_instance.primary` for clarity, runs apply — and Terraform destroys the production database and creates a new empty one. No moved block was used.
evidence: renamed aws_db_instance.main -> .primary; apply destroyed prod DB.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the prevention?
choices: Renaming the address changed the resource's identity — Terraform saw 'delete main, create primary' (addresses ARE identity). Prevention: the moved block (declares the rename as a state operation — plan shows 'moved' not destroy/create), plus the workflow (plan before apply would have shown the destroy; prevent_destroy on the database would have blocked it). Three independent guardrails, all missing.
Terraform is dangerous; avoid renames.
The engineer should have known.
Restoring from backup is the fix.
scenarios.hint: A rename destroyed a production database — what happened and what prevents it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the identity mechanism (addresses are identity), gives the primary prevention (moved blocks) plus the two backup guardrails (plan review, prevent_destroy) — defense in depth. B/C blame or avoid; D is recovery, not prevention.

domains.name: Terraform State Deep Dive
domains.description: State files, locking, backends, drift, and the operations of state surgery.

scenarios.title: The Forgotten Orphan
scenarios.situation: An engineer hand-edits the state file to 'remove' a resource they deleted manually in the console. Now Terraform wants to CREATE the resource (it thinks it's new), while the actual resource still exists — and the next apply will collide.
evidence: hand-edited state; terraform plans CREATE for an existing resource.
choices: Hand-editing broke the mapping: the state is the config↔reality link — editing it by hand desynced Terraform's memory without touching reality. The correct removal of a manually-deleted resource is `terraform state rm` (tells Terraform to forget it deliberately, recorded properly) or `terraform import` (re-links reality to config). The rule: state mutations go through terraform state subcommands, which maintain the file's integrity — text editors don't.
The state file is corrupted; delete it.
Terraform can't handle manual changes.
Recreate everything.
scenarios.hint: Hand-editing state to remove a resource desyncs Terraform — what went wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the mapping-break mechanism and gives the two proper tools (state rm for forgetting, import for re-linking) plus the integrity principle. B destroys the memory; C/D surrender.

scenarios.title: The Corrupted Monday
scenarios.situation: Two engineers run apply simultaneously against local state on a shared drive. Monday morning, half the resources are 'forgotten' — Terraform plans to recreate production infrastructure.
evidence: 2 simultaneous applies, shared-drive state; Monday: half resources 'forgotten.'
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
choices: Concurrent writes without locking corrupted the state: two processes wrote the JSON simultaneously, producing a merged file that lost resource mappings — the 'forgotten' resources are still real, just unremembered. Immediate: STOP all applies, restore from backup/versioned copy, reconcile with terraform refresh/import. Structural: remote backend (S3) with DynamoDB locking — the mutex that makes concurrent applies serialize instead of corrupt. And never local state on shared storage.
Terraform lost the resources; recreate them.
The engineers should coordinate better.
Shared drives are fine with care.
scenarios.hint: Concurrent applies corrupt local state; Terraform 'forgets' prod — what happened and what fixes it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It explains the corruption mechanism (concurrent JSON writes), gives the immediate recovery (stop, restore, reconcile) and the structural fix (remote backend + locking) — incident response plus prevention. B destroys; C/D wishful.

scenarios.title: The Mystery Diff
scenarios.situation: Every morning, `terraform plan` shows changes to an ECS service's desired_count that nobody made. The team 'fixes' it by reverting via apply — and the next morning it's back. This has gone on for weeks.
evidence: plan shows desired_count changes daily; apply reverts; returns next day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual problem and fix?
choices: The desired_count is owned by the autoscaler (Application Auto Scaling adjusts it based on metrics) — Terraform and the autoscaler are fighting over the same argument, and Terraform 'wins' each morning only to lose again by afternoon. The fix: `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_count] }` — the declared truce for an externally-owned argument. The weeks of reverting were fighting the wrong battle: the config was wrong (claiming ownership), not the world.
The autoscaler is broken.
Someone is changing it secretly.
Keep reverting; it'll stabilize.
scenarios.hint: Terraform fights the autoscaler over desired_count every morning — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the ownership conflict (two controllers, one argument), gives the exact fix (ignore_changes as declared truce), and reframes the weeks of reverting (config wrong, not world). B/C misdiagnose; D perpetuates.

scenarios.title: The Accidental Import
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs `terraform import` with the wrong resource ID, then applies — Terraform now manages (and modifies) a production resource it was never meant to touch. The state maps the address to the wrong real object.
evidence: import with wrong ID; apply modified unintended prod resource.
choices: `terraform state rm` the wrongly-mapped address (removes the mapping WITHOUT destroying — the production resource is untouched, just unmanaged again), verify with `terraform state list` and plan (should show the intended create, not modifications to prod), then import with the CORRECT ID and write matching config. The rm-before-reimport sequence is the key: fix the mapping before any apply touches reality again.
Destroy and recreate the prod resource.
Hand-edit the state JSON.
Leave it; it's managed now.
scenarios.hint: A wrong-ID import now manages the wrong production resource — what is the recovery?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the exact recovery sequence (rm the bad mapping → verify → reimport correctly), emphasizes the no-destroy semantics of rm, and orders operations to protect reality. B destroys; C corrupts; D surrenders.

scenarios.title: The Prod Apply
scenarios.situation: A CI job runs `terraform workspace select prod` then apply — but an earlier step failed silently, the select never ran, and the job applied the production config to the dev workspace state. Dev is now running prod-sized infrastructure (and billing).
evidence: select prod failed silently; apply ran against dev workspace.
choices: Eliminate workspace selection from CI: use directory separation (envs/dev, envs/prod as separate configurations with separate backend keys) so the environment is structural, not a runtime selection — or at minimum, assert `terraform workspace show` matches the intended environment and fail the job otherwise. The lesson: environment identity must be impossible to get wrong, not merely unlikely — interactive state in automation is the defect.
Be more careful with CI steps.
Workspaces are fine; the script had a bug.
Merge dev and prod.
scenarios.hint: A failed select applied prod config to dev state — what is the structural fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It makes environment identity structural (directories) rather than runtime (select), adds the assertion guard as minimum, and states the principle (impossible, not unlikely). B/C blame or excuse; D is absurd.

scenarios.title: The Auditor's Question
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks: 'Who accessed the production Terraform state in the last 90 days, and were any secrets in it?' The team has no access logging, broad bucket read access, and database passwords in variables.
evidence: no logging, broad reads, DB passwords in variables; auditor asks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest answer and the remediation?
choices: Honest answer: 'we can't say who accessed it, and yes, secrets are in it' — the two failures (no audit trail, secrets in state) stated plainly. Remediation: enable access logging + CloudTrail immediately (future questions answerable), tighten the bucket policy to CI + break-glass, rotate all exposed secrets, migrate to dynamic credentials (Vault/AWS Secrets Manager references), enable versioning + MFA delete. The roadmap is unglamorous and complete — and the honesty is what makes the auditor trust the fix.
Claim no one accessed it.
Delete the state and start over.
Secrets in state are fine.
scenarios.hint: An auditor asks who accessed prod state and whether secrets are in it — what is the answer?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the honest answer first (the credibility move), then the complete unglamorous remediation in priority order — logging, access, rotation, dynamic credentials, versioning. B lies; C destroys; D denies.

domains.name: Terraform Modules
domains.description: Module authoring, composition, versioning, and the registry ecosystem.

scenarios.title: The Missing Output
scenarios.situation: A team authors a VPC module but forgets to output the subnet IDs. Every caller works around it with a `data "aws_subnets"` lookup — duplicating the filter logic in six root configs, which drift apart over months.
evidence: VPC module: no subnet outputs; 6 roots with duplicated aws_subnets filters.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix and the principle?
choices: Add the outputs to the module (subnet IDs, VPC ID, route table IDs — everything the module creates that callers need) and refactor the six workarounds to reference them. The principle: the module's interface is complete only when callers never need data-source workarounds for the module's own resources — outputs are the return values, and an incomplete return is an incomplete API. The drifted filters get deleted, not maintained.
Keep the data lookups; they work.
Each caller should maintain its own filters.
The module is fine as-is.
scenarios.hint: A VPC module lacks subnet outputs; six callers duplicate data lookups — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the incomplete-API mechanism (missing returns forcing workarounds), prescribes the interface completion plus workaround removal, and states the principle. B/C/D accept the drift.

scenarios.title: The Circular Wire
scenarios.situation: Module A's output feeds module B, and module B's output feeds module A — Terraform errors with a cycle. The team 'fixes' it by merging both modules into one giant module.
evidence: cycle: module.a -> module.b -> module.a; team merged them.
choices: Restructure to break the cycle: extract the shared dependency into a foundation module C that both A and B consume (A and B become siblings, not spouses). The merge-'fix' creates a god module with a huge blast radius — the cycle was telling them the layering was wrong, and the right response is re-layering (foundation → consumers), not consolidation. Cycles are architecture feedback.
Merging is correct; cycles mean modules are too small.
Use depends_on to order the cycle.
Cycles are fine; ignore the error.
scenarios.hint: Two modules feed each other in a cycle — what is the better fix than merging?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reads the cycle as architecture feedback, gives the re-layering fix (shared foundation, sibling consumers), and rejects the god-module merge. B misreads; C can't order cycles; D ignores.

scenarios.title: The Breaking Minor
scenarios.situation: A module author renames `instance_type` to `size` in v2.3.0 (a minor release). Twenty caller configs break on the next init. The author says 'the new name is better.'
evidence: v2.3.0 renames instance_type -> size; 20 callers break.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rule that was violated?
choices: Semantic versioning: renaming an input is a BREAKING change — it belongs in a MAJOR version (v3.0.0), with the old variable deprecated (not removed) for a full major cycle. The 'better name' doesn't excuse the contract break: twenty callers' plans are the cost of the author's aesthetics. The fix: yank or re-release as v3.0.0, restore instance_type as deprecated in the 2.x line, document the migration.
Better names justify breaking changes.
Callers should pin exact versions.
Minor versions can break things.
scenarios.hint: A module rename in a minor release breaks 20 callers — what rule was violated?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It states the semver rule precisely (input rename = major), gives the remediation (re-release as major, deprecate don't remove), and prices the violation (twenty broken callers). B/C/D excuse or misplace.

scenarios.title: The Abandoned Module
scenarios.situation: A team built on a registry module with 3M downloads — last commit 3 years ago, 200 open issues, incompatible with the current provider major. Upgrading the provider is now blocked.
evidence: 3M downloads; 3 years stale; 200 issues; blocks provider 6.x.
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson and the path forward?
choices: Downloads are not maintenance: the evaluation criteria (recent commits, issue responsiveness, version currency) were the real signals, and popularity masked abandonment. Path forward: fork and maintain (if the module is central), migrate to a maintained alternative (the terraform-aws-modules current line), or vendor-and-own (copy into your repo, take responsibility). And the process fix: module selection criteria documented and re-evaluated on provider upgrades — dependencies get reviewed, not just installed.
Popularity equals quality; keep waiting.
Never use public modules.
The provider shouldn't have upgraded.
scenarios.hint: An abandoned-but-popular module blocks a provider upgrade — what is the lesson and path?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the signal failure (popularity masked abandonment), gives the three concrete paths (fork, migrate, vendor), and adds the process fix (selection criteria, re-evaluation). B/C/D all avoid.

scenarios.title: The Atomic Change
scenarios.situation: A network change (new subnet) requires a coordinated app change (new subnet IDs) — but they're in separate repos with separate CI. The network PR merges Monday, the app PR merges Thursday; Tuesday-Wednesday the app is broken.
evidence: network PR Mon, app PR Thu; app broken Tue-Wed.
scenarios.prompt: What does this reveal about the repo choice?
choices: The coordination cost of polyrepo: cross-component atomicity is the monorepo's core advantage, and this incident priced it (3 days broken). The options: merge into a monorepo (atomic PRs), or keep polyrepo with contract discipline (network change held until app PR is ready — coordinated release trains, versioned outputs as the interface). The reveal: the repo layout must match the change-coupling — tightly-coupled components want one repo (or release-train discipline).
Polyrepo is always wrong.
The app team was too slow.
Never change networks.
scenarios.hint: Cross-repo changes break the app for 3 days — what does this reveal?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It prices the coordination failure, gives both structural options (monorepo atomicity or polyrepo release-train discipline), and states the principle (layout matches change-coupling). B/C/D all miss.

scenarios.title: The Untested Change
scenarios.situation: A module author changes the S3 module's default (versioning off → on, for compliance). Ten caller configs break — they were explicitly setting versioning=false and the new validation rejects it. No test caught the contract change.
evidence: default change; 10 callers break; no test caught it.
scenarios.prompt: What would the testing pyramid have done?
choices: The plan-level and Terratest gates would have caught it: the example configs (as fixtures) applying with the new default would show the validation failures in CI — the contract change visible BEFORE merge. The pyramid's value here isn't the apply test (the breakage is at plan time) but the examples-as-fixtures discipline: every example must apply clean, so a contract-breaking default breaks CI loudly. The ten callers get a migration note in the changelog, not a surprise.
Don't change defaults.
The callers were wrong.
Tests can't catch this.
scenarios.hint: A module default change breaks 10 callers uncaught — what would testing have done?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It shows exactly which pyramid level catches it (examples-as-fixtures at plan time), gives the process fix (changelog migration note), and distinguishes the test levels' roles. B/C/D avoid the discipline.

domains.name: Terraform Cloud & Enterprise
domains.description: Managed runs, VCS workflows, speculative plans, and collaboration at scale.

scenarios.title: The Laptop Apply
scenarios.situation: An engineer applies prod from their laptop with local credentials; the apply partially fails; the state is now half-updated and only on their machine. The team can't tell what ran.
objectives: Map each failure to its fix
evidence: laptop apply, partial failure, state local-only, no audit trail.
choices: Everything about this incident: remote execution runs on TFC's runners (consistent environment — no laptop variance), with the workspace's credentials (the engineer never holds prod keys — credential isolation), native workspace locking (no concurrent corruption), and full run history (what ran, who triggered, the exact plan — the audit trail). The laptop apply is the anti-pattern remote execution was built to kill: unrepeatable, unaudited, unshared.
Laptops need better specs.
The engineer should be more careful.
Local state is fine with backups.
scenarios.hint: A laptop prod apply half-fails with state only local — what does remote execution fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It maps each failure mode to the specific remote-execution fix (environment, credentials, locking, history) and names the anti-pattern. B/C/D treat symptoms.

scenarios.title: The Blind Merge
scenarios.situation: A PR adding 'one small security group rule' merges without anyone reading the speculative plan. The rule opens 0.0.0.0/0 to the database port — the plan check showed it clearly, but nobody looked. Production data is exposed for 6 hours.
evidence: 'one small SG rule' -> 0.0.0.0/0 on DB port; plan check unread; 6h exposure.
choices: The review process, not the tooling: the speculative plan DID its job (showed the 0.0.0.0/0 rule as a PR check) — the humans skipped the infrastructure diff. The fixes: required plan-check review (CODEOWNERS on the IaC paths + the plan output as required reading), policy-as-code that would have BLOCKED the 0.0.0.0/0 rule automatically (the policy topic's territory), and the cultural point — the plan output is the diff that matters, not the HCL. Tooling provided the safety; process bypassed it.
Terraform Cloud failed.
Speculative plans don't work.
Small PRs don't need review.
scenarios.hint: A merged PR exposes the DB; the plan check showed it but nobody read it — what failed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It locates the failure precisely (humans skipped the working tool), gives the layered fixes (required review, policy-as-code blocking, cultural), and states the principle (plan output is the diff). B/C blame the tool; D excuses.

scenarios.title: The Rotation Nightmare
scenarios.situation: AWS credentials are pasted as workspace variables in 40 workspaces. The key leaks; rotation means editing 40 workspaces by hand — taking hours, during which the old key is still live in the ones not yet updated.
evidence: key leaked; 40 workspaces with pasted creds; rotation ongoing for hours.
choices: Variable sets: one credentials set attached to all 40 workspaces — rotation becomes a single update, atomic across the fleet. And the deeper fix: Vault dynamic secrets (short-lived credentials minted per run — nothing long-lived to leak or rotate). The incident priced the duplication: 40 hand-edits during an active leak is the failure mode variable sets exist to prevent. Migrate now, rotate once, never again.
Rotate faster next time.
Fewer workspaces.
The key shouldn't have leaked.
scenarios.hint: Leaked credentials live in 40 workspaces; rotation takes hours — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the structural fix (variable sets: one update, atomic), the deeper fix (Vault dynamic secrets: nothing to leak), and prices the incident (hand-edits during active leak). B/C/D treat symptoms.

scenarios.title: The Blocked Friday
scenarios.situation: A new mandatory run task (security scanner) blocks 30 runs on a Friday — including the hotfix for an active incident. The task was enabled as mandatory on day one with no advisory period. Teams are furious; the security team says 'policy is policy.'
evidence: mandatory scanner day one; 30 blocked incl. incident hotfix; no exceptions.
choices: The rollout, not the policy: mandatory-on-day-one with no advisory period meant no calibration (false-positive rate unknown), no exceptions path (incident hotfixes need break-glass), and no trust (teams experienced the gate as ambush). The fix: revert to advisory, measure the would-block rate for two weeks, tune the scanner, define the break-glass exception (incident + post-hoc review), THEN go mandatory. Gates need legitimacy — legitimacy comes from calibration and exceptions.
Security should override everything.
The teams are wrong to be angry.
Remove the scanner.
scenarios.hint: A day-one mandatory scanner blocks 30 runs including an incident hotfix — what went wrong?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It diagnoses the rollout failure (no calibration, no exceptions, no trust), gives the recovery sequence (advisory → tune → break-glass → mandatory), and states the legitimacy principle. B/C side with the ambush; D surrenders.

scenarios.title: The Queued Monday
scenarios.situation: Monday morning: 50 runs queued, none executing. The agent pool's VMs were reclaimed by the autoscaler over the weekend (scale-to-zero policy). Nobody was alerted — the queue just grew.
evidence: scale-to-zero reclaimed agents; 50 queued, no alert.
choices: Alert on queue depth (the leading indicator — runs waiting, not agents dead), set a minimum agent count (scale-to-zero is wrong for the execution plane — keep N warm), and make the autoscaler queue-aware (scale on pending runs, not just CPU). The deeper lesson: the execution plane is production infrastructure — it gets production monitoring (SLOs on run start latency), not best-effort treatment. The queue is the canary.
Disable autoscaling entirely.
Agents are unreliable; go back to local.
Manually start agents Mondays.
scenarios.hint: An autoscaler reclaims all agents over the weekend; Monday 50 runs queue silently — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the three fixes (queue-depth alerting, warm minimum, queue-aware scaling) and the framing (execution plane = production infrastructure with SLOs). B/C/D overcorrect or ritualize.

scenarios.title: The $40k NAT Gateway
scenarios.situation: A PR adds a NAT gateway per AZ (3×) for a dev environment. The cost estimate shows +$3,400/mo (+$40k/yr) — for dev. Nobody would have noticed without the estimate; the gate blocks it pending review.
evidence: 3x NAT gateway for dev; +$3,400/mo; nobody noticed until estimate.
choices: Cost visibility at decision time: the $40k/yr was invisible in the HCL (three small resource blocks) but obvious in the cost diff — the estimate translates architecture into money before the bill. The gate's value isn't blocking (dev might legitimately need it) but forcing the conversation ('do we need per-AZ NAT in dev, or a single NAT?') — the FinOps discipline: every expensive choice made deliberately, with the number attached.
NAT gateways are too expensive.
Dev doesn't need networking.
The gate should auto-reject.
scenarios.hint: A dev PR quietly adds $40k/yr in NAT gateways — what does cost estimation change?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It shows the translation value (HCL hides cost, the diff reveals it), frames the gate as conversation-forcer not auto-rejecter, and gives the concrete alternative (single NAT for dev). B/C/D miss the discipline.

domains.name: ArgoCD GitOps Mastery
domains.description: ArgoCD deep dive: Applications, sync, App of Apps, projects, and multi-cluster.

scenarios.title: The Unhealed Drift
scenarios.situation: An engineer hotfixes production with kubectl (scales a deployment manually). ArgoCD has no selfHeal enabled. Weeks later, nobody remembers the manual change — and the next git sync doesn't revert it because the manifests were never updated.
evidence: manual scale via kubectl; no selfHeal; forgotten in weeks.
choices: `selfHeal: true` in the automated sync policy — the continuous-reconciliation contract: ArgoCD would have reverted the manual scale within minutes, forcing the hotfix into git (where it belongs) instead of letting it fossilize as tribal knowledge. The deeper lesson: without self-heal, 'GitOps' is git-as-suggestion — the drift the existing scenario catalogued ('Drift that nobody noticed') is the predictable outcome. Enable self-heal; route hotfixes through git.
kubectl should be banned.
The engineer should have remembered.
Manual changes are fine.
scenarios.hint: A kubectl hotfix fossilizes because ArgoCD lacks selfHeal — what is missing?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the exact missing flag, explains the forcing function (hotfixes must go through git), and connects to the drift scenario — the reconciliation contract made concrete. B/C/D moralize or surrender.

scenarios.title: The Fifty-App Toil
scenarios.situation: A team manages 50 microservices as 50 hand-written Application manifests. Adding a service means copy-paste-edit; a field rename means 50 edits; three are now out of sync with the template and nobody knows which.
evidence: 50 hand-written Apps; 3 drifted from template; renames = 50 edits.
choices: ApplicationSet with the Git generator: one manifest generating all 50 Applications from the directory structure — adding a service becomes adding a directory (the generator does the rest), field changes happen once (in the template), and drift-from-template becomes impossible (there's only one template). The three out-of-sync apps get regenerated correctly on the next reconciliation. Manual multi-app management is the toil ApplicationSets were built to eliminate.
Hire someone to manage the 50 files.
Fewer microservices.
The template drift is fine.
scenarios.hint: 50 hand-written Applications drift from their template — what is the structural fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the structural fix (generator + template), shows how each pain point resolves (add = directory, rename = once, drift = impossible), and names the toil. B/C/D avoid or surrender.

scenarios.title: The Cross-Team Delete
scenarios.situation: Team A's ArgoCD Application (in the default project, prune enabled) is misconfigured with a too-broad path — and prunes Team B's production namespace. There were no guardrails: default project, cluster-admin-ish access, no scoping.
objectives: Map each to the missing layer
evidence: default project, broad path, prune: team B's prod namespace deleted.
choices: AppProjects per team (scoped destinations — Team A's apps physically can't target Team B's namespaces), RBAC least-privilege (sync rights only within the project), CI policy on manifests (conftest blocking default-project apps and over-broad paths), and prune discipline (prune enabled only with scoped projects). The incident was the 'no guardrails' scenario realized — every layer missing. Defense in depth: scoping + RBAC + CI gates + prune hygiene.
Disable prune everywhere.
Team A should be more careful.
One team per cluster.
scenarios.hint: A misconfigured prune deletes another team's namespace — what are the layered defenses?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It stacks the four defenses (projects, RBAC, CI policy, prune discipline) and maps each to the incident's missing layer — defense in depth, not a single fix. B overcorrects; C blames; D is expensive.

scenarios.title: Latest Strikes Again
scenarios.situation: Production runs `image: web:latest`. A registry push at 2 AM deploys untested code to prod — ArgoCD didn't even sync (the tag didn't change, just its content). Rollback means guessing which digest was live.
evidence: web:latest; 2AM push deploys untested; rollback = guess digest.
choices: Image Updater + tag discipline: pin immutable tags (semver or digest — the tag names the artifact), let the updater bump tags via git commits (tested images promoted deliberately), and ban `latest` by policy (conftest/kyverno blocking `:latest` in prod). Rollback becomes `git revert`. The 2 AM surprise is structurally impossible when tags are immutable and changes flow through git — the existing scenario's lesson, enforced by tooling.
Don't push at 2 AM.
latest is fine with care.
Pin digests manually forever.
scenarios.hint: A 2 AM latest push deploys untested code; rollback is guesswork — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the structural fix (immutable tags + updater + policy ban), explains why the incident becomes impossible (content-addressed, git-flowed), and makes rollback a git revert. B/C moralize; D is toil.

scenarios.title: The Lost Control Plane
scenarios.situation: The management cluster running ArgoCD suffers total failure. The team realizes: ArgoCD's own configuration was applied by hand months ago, the root app manifest lives on someone's laptop, and nobody has ever rebuilt it.
evidence: mgmt cluster lost; ArgoCD config hand-applied; root app on laptop.
scenarios.prompt: What is the recovery and the prevention?
choices: Recovery: reinstall ArgoCD (Helm chart), re-register clusters, re-apply Applications from the git repos (the desired state survived — it's all in git), verify convergence cluster by cluster. Prevention: the root app + ArgoCD's own config IN GIT (the bootstrap repo), Velero backups of the argocd namespace, and the quarterly game-day (rebuild drill) — the control plane gets the same GitOps discipline as the workloads. 'GitOps managing GitOps' isn't philosophy; it's the DR plan.
Rebuild everything by hand.
The cluster is lost; start over.
ArgoCD doesn't need backup.
scenarios.hint: Total ArgoCD failure with config only on a laptop — what is the recovery and prevention?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the recovery sequence (reinstall → re-register → re-apply from git → verify), the three preventions (config in git, Velero, game-days), and the principle (control plane gets GitOps discipline too). B/C/D surrender or deny.

scenarios.title: The Fork Leak
scenarios.situation: The GitOps repo is public (open-source project). A contributor forks it — including a plaintext database password committed months ago ('temporary'). The fork is public; the password is now on the internet.
evidence: public repo; fork contains plaintext DB password from months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the response and the structural fix?
choices: Response: ROTATE immediately (the password is public — history rewrites don't recall forks), purge from history, audit for other plaintext. Structural: Sealed Secrets or SOPS mandatory (the pre-commit hook blocking unsealed secrets — gitleaks + a custom check), so 'temporary' plaintext becomes structurally impossible. The public repo makes the discipline non-negotiable: ciphertext in git, always — the fork contains nothing usable.
Make the repo private.
Delete the fork.
The password was temporary; it's fine.
scenarios.hint: A public repo fork leaks a committed plaintext password — what is the response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It treats the exposure as a rotation event (forks can't be recalled), gives the immediate steps, and the structural prevention (mandatory encryption + pre-commit gates). B/C/D misunderstand git's distribution.

domains.name: Flux GitOps
domains.description: Flux v2: sources, reconcilers, image automation, and multi-tenancy.

scenarios.title: The Silent Suspend
scenarios.situation: An engineer suspends a Kustomization for debugging on Friday, forgets, and leaves. Monday's critical security patch merges to git — and never reaches the cluster. Tuesday's incident response discovers the app is three versions behind.
evidence: suspend Fri, forgotten; security patch never deployed; found Tue.
choices: Alert on suspended resources (the notification-controller or a policy check: any Kustomization/HelmRelease suspended > N hours pages), plus the cultural rule (suspend is a debugging tool with a timebox — the engineer notes the resume time when suspending). The deeper fix: make suspension visible (dashboard, Slack alerts on suspend events) — invisible state changes are the failure mode. The patch was in git; the loop was paused; nobody knew.
Never suspend anything.
The engineer should remember better.
Suspension is broken.
scenarios.hint: A forgotten Friday suspend blocks Monday's security patch — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the detection (alert on suspended > N hours), the cultural rule (timeboxed suspend), and the visibility principle — the operational fix for invisible state. B/C/D moralize or ban.

scenarios.title: The Stuck Bad Release
scenarios.situation: A HelmRelease upgrade deploys a crashing image. No remediation is configured. The release sits broken; the on-call engineer doesn't know Flux manages it and tries kubectl fixes — which Flux reverts on the next interval, confusing everyone.
evidence: bad image via HelmRelease; no remediation; kubectl fixes reverted.
choices: Configure `remediation: { remediateLastFailure: true }` (automatic rollback of failed upgrades — the release self-heals), and fix the operational visibility (labels/annotations showing Flux management, runbook entry, notification-controller alerts on HelmRelease failures). The incident had two gaps: no automatic remediation AND nobody knew the controller owned the release — automation without observability is the failure mode.
Flux shouldn't manage Helm.
The engineer should have known.
Disable Flux reconciliation.
scenarios.hint: A crashing HelmRelease sits broken; kubectl fixes get reverted confusingly — what are the fixes?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives both fixes (remediation config + operational visibility), names the compound failure (no self-heal + unknown ownership), and states the principle (automation needs observability). B/C/D retreat or blame.

scenarios.title: The Breaking Minor
scenarios.situation: Image automation with policy `semver: 1.x` promotes 1.3.0 automatically — which contains a breaking API change. Production breaks at 3 AM. The policy was 'automate everything.'
evidence: policy semver:1.x; 1.3.0 auto-promoted with breaking change; 3AM outage.
choices: Narrow the automation to patch (`semver: 1.2.x` — the safe, backward-compatible range) and gate minors/majors behind human promotion (PR-based: the automation detects, a human approves the minor bump). The principle: automation for the safe (patches), humans for the risky (minors/majors) — the deliberate-gate design. 'Automate everything' automated the breaking change too.
Disable image automation.
The image publisher shouldn't break APIs.
Pin one tag forever.
scenarios.hint: Image automation promotes a breaking minor at 3 AM — what is the policy fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the precise policy fix (patch-range automation, human-gated minors), states the deliberate-gate principle, and diagnoses the over-automation. B/D retreat; C blames upstream.

scenarios.title: The Leaked Secret
scenarios.situation: A developer commits a plaintext database password to the GitOps repo ('just for testing'). It's now in git history forever — cloned to every developer laptop, visible in every fork.
evidence: 'just for testing' plaintext password committed; cloned widely.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate and structural response?
choices: Immediate: ROTATE the credential (it's compromised — history can't be uncloned; rewriting history doesn't recall the clones), purge from history (BFG/filter-repo) to reduce future exposure, audit access. Structural: SOPS (or external-secrets) made mandatory by policy (pre-commit hook blocking plaintext secrets + CI check), so 'just for testing' becomes structurally impossible. The secret in history is a rotation event, not a cleanup event.
Delete the commit; it's fine.
Rewrite history; the clones don't matter.
Secrets in git are okay if the repo is private.
scenarios.hint: A plaintext DB password is committed to the GitOps repo — what is the response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It states the hard truth (rotation, not cleanup — clones can't be recalled), gives the immediate steps, and the structural prevention (SOPS mandatory + pre-commit/CI gates). B/C/D misunderstand git's permanence.

scenarios.title: The Quiet Failure
scenarios.situation: A Kustomization has been failing reconciliation for 6 days. Nobody noticed — no alerts configured, the dashboard unviewed, the git commits flowing normally (the source was fine; the cluster apply was failing).
evidence: Kustomization failing 6 days; git healthy; no alerts; unviewed dashboard.
choices: No failure alerting on the reconciliation loop: the git side was healthy (commits flowing) but the cluster side was broken — and nothing watched the gap between desired and actual. The fix: Alert on error-severity Kustomization/HelmRelease events (paging), a reconciliation-health dashboard (failing resources, sorted by age), and the SLO (time from git commit to converged — the GitOps latency metric). GitOps without reconciliation observability is hope-based deployment.
The Kustomization was misconfigured.
Someone should check dashboards daily.
Flux is unreliable.
scenarios.hint: A Kustomization fails silently for 6 days — what is the observability gap?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the gap precisely (nothing watched desired-vs-actual), gives the three fixes (alerts, dashboard, SLO), and states the principle (reconciliation needs observability). B blames config; C ritualizes; D blames the tool.

scenarios.title: The Twelve Directories
scenarios.situation: Twelve environments, twelve full copies of the manifests. A security label added to eleven; the twelfth missed — and its pods run unlabeled for months. Nobody knows which dirs differ anymore.
evidence: 12 full copies; label added to 11; 12th unlabeled for months.
choices: Base + overlays: one base holding everything common (the label added once), twelve tiny overlays holding only differences (replicas, domains, the values). The missed label becomes impossible (it's in the base — inherited everywhere); the 'which dirs differ' question answers itself (the overlays ARE the differences, each a few lines). The copy-paste drift factory gets demolished by the structure — customization without duplication.
Add the label to the twelfth dir.
Fewer environments.
A script to sync the dirs.
scenarios.hint: Twelve copied manifest dirs drift; one misses a security label for months — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the structural fix (base+overlays), shows how each pain resolves (missed label impossible, differences self-documenting), and names the anti-pattern (the drift factory). B/C/D patch the symptom.

domains.name: Policy as Code
domains.description: Guardrails for IaC and GitOps: OPA, Kyverno, Sentinel, and admission control.

scenarios.title: The Friday Block
scenarios.situation: A new Conftest policy (written that morning, untested) blocks ALL Friday deploys — including the incident hotfix. The Rego has a logic error: it denies every S3 bucket instead of just unencrypted ones. It was enabled as a blocking check immediately.
evidence: morning-written Rego, day-one blocking; denies all S3; hotfix blocked.
choices: Untested policy (no opa test with allow/deny cases — the logic error would have been caught) AND no gradual rollout (blocking on day one with no advisory period — the run-tasks lesson's rollout pattern applies to policy too). The fix: revert to advisory, add the test cases, tune, then enforce — plus the break-glass exception for incident hotfixes. Policy gates need the same legitimacy as any gate: tested, calibrated, escapable in emergencies.
Policy as code doesn't work.
The hotfix should have waited.
Delete all policies.
scenarios.hint: An untested policy blocks all Friday deploys including a hotfix — what are the failures?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names both failures (untested + no gradual rollout), gives the recovery sequence, and connects to the gate-legitimacy principle — the policy version of the run-tasks lesson. B/D surrender; C delays the incident.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Mutation
scenarios.situation: A Kyverno mutate rule (new, untested) rewrites every Deployment's image pull policy at midnight — breaking the team's air-gapped registry setup (images now pull Always from the unreachable public registry). Hundreds of pods crash-loop.
evidence: new mutate rule, immediate enforce; pull policy rewritten; mass crash-loop.
choices: Untested mutation with immediate enforcement: mutate rules CHANGE resources (unlike validate's admit/deny) — an untested mutation is an automated incident generator. The failures: no kyverno test cases, no Audit-mode observation period, no canary (one namespace first). The fix: revert the policy, run in Audit, test the mutation's effects, canary one namespace, then enforce fleet-wide. Mutations get MORE caution than validations, not less — they act, not just judge.
Kyverno is dangerous.
Mutations should be banned.
The registry team should fix their setup.
scenarios.hint: An untested Kyverno mutation breaks hundreds of pods at midnight — what failed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It distinguishes mutation risk (acts vs judges), names the three missing safeguards (tests, Audit period, canary), and gives the recovery sequence — mutations deserve more caution. B/C ban the tool; D blames.

scenarios.title: The Overridden Gate
scenarios.situation: A soft-mandatory Sentinel policy (no public S3 buckets) is overridden 47 times in a month — always with reason 'needed for demo.' The policy is now decoration; the security team wants hard-mandatory everywhere.
objectives: Encode or enforce, don't just harden
evidence: 47 overrides/month, all 'needed for demo'; security wants hard-mandatory.
choices: The override rate IS the signal: 47 'demo' overrides mean the policy doesn't match reality (demos legitimately need public buckets — the policy needs a scoped exception: demo workspaces tagged, time-boxed, auto-remediated) OR the culture ignores gates (then hard-mandatory just moves the bypass elsewhere). The analysis: audit the 47 (legitimate pattern? → encode the exception; laziness? → enforce + educate). Hard-mandatory everywhere without the analysis punishes the legitimate demos and teaches circumvention.
Make it hard-mandatory; overrides are bad.
Remove the policy; it's ignored.
The demo team is the problem.
scenarios.hint: A soft-mandatory policy is overridden 47 times as 'demo' — what is the analysis?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reads the override rate as data (not disobedience), gives the diagnostic fork (encode the legitimate pattern vs enforce the real rule), and warns that blind hardening teaches circumvention. B/C/D skip the analysis.

scenarios.title: The Blocked Cluster
scenarios.situation: A Kyverno webhook pod crashes (OOM). failurePolicy is Fail (the default). Every Deployment apply in the cluster now hangs and fails — including the fix for the webhook itself (which needs to apply the fixed Deployment).
evidence: Kyverno OOM; failurePolicy Fail; all applies hang incl. the fix.
scenarios.prompt: What is the recovery and the prevention?
choices: Recovery: delete or bypass the webhook configuration (kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration — the break-glass, documented in the runbook) to unblock the API, then fix and redeploy. Prevention: resource limits tuned (the OOM's cause), webhook HA (replicas + PDB), failurePolicy chosen per webhook (Ignore for the non-critical, Fail only where safety demands), and the runbook with the break-glass steps — practiced, not just written. The deadlock (can't fix the fixer) is the failurePolicy: Fail trap.
The cluster is bricked; rebuild it.
failurePolicy: Fail is always correct.
Webhooks are too risky.
scenarios.hint: A crashed webhook with failurePolicy: Fail deadlocks the cluster — what is the recovery?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the break-glass recovery (delete the webhook config), the three preventions (resources, HA, deliberate failurePolicy), and names the deadlock pattern — the Fail-trap diagnosed. B/C/D surrender or dogmatize.

scenarios.title: The Rotted Policy
scenarios.situation: A two-year-old policy blocks a new instance family the company now standardizes on. No owner, no review cadence, no kill switch documented — the team spends a day finding who can disable it (nobody knows).
evidence: 2-year-old policy blocks new standard; no owner; day-long disable hunt.
choices: Policy ownership hygiene: every policy gets an owner, a quarterly review cadence (policies rot as infrastructure evolves — the instance-family drift is the predictable rot), and a documented kill switch. The immediate fix (disable/update the policy) is trivial once someone owns it — the day-long search was the real incident. Add the policy inventory (all gates, owners, last-reviewed) to the platform's operational docs.
Policies shouldn't restrict instance types.
The new instance family is wrong.
Delete old policies periodically.
scenarios.hint: A rotted ownerless policy blocks the new standard; nobody can disable it — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the systemic failure (ownerless, unreviewed, no kill switch), gives the hygiene model (owner + cadence + kill switch + inventory), and identifies the real incident (the search, not the block). B/C/D dodge.

scenarios.title: The Hour-Late Gate
scenarios.situation: Policy checks run only in the TFC run pipeline — 45 minutes after the PR opens. Developers merge without waiting ('the check takes too long'), then the run fails, then they fix, then re-run: the 2-hour policy loop. Adoption is zero; resentment is high.
evidence: TFC-only gates, 45-min delay; merges without waiting; 2-hr fix loop.
choices: Shift the fast policies left: Conftest in CI on the PR (minutes, not 45) for the syntactic/universal checks (encryption, tags, no-latest), keeping the TFC run gates for the blast-radius-aware policies (cost, cross-workspace). The 2-hour loop becomes a 5-minute loop for the common cases — and the run gate stays as the authoritative backstop. Speed is the adoption lever: the gate developers don't wait for is the gate they bypass.
Make the TFC runs faster.
Remove the policies.
Developers should wait.
scenarios.hint: Policy feedback takes 2 hours; developers bypass it — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It splits the gates by speed-sensitivity (fast/universal left, blast-radius-aware at run), quantifies the loop improvement (2hr → 5min), and names the adoption mechanism (speed). B/C/D keep the slow loop.

domains.name: Ansible & Terraform Together
domains.description: Configuration management alongside provisioning: roles, inventory, and the handoff.

scenarios.title: The Provisioner Config
scenarios.situation: A team configures 200 servers with Terraform remote-exec provisioners (installing packages, writing configs, starting services). Drift is rampant (manual fixes never re-applied), reruns do nothing, and onboarding takes days of provisioner debugging.
evidence: 200 servers, remote-exec config; drift; reruns no-op; slow onboarding.
choices: Move configuration to Ansible: Terraform provisions the 200 instances (its strength — state, drift detection, lifecycle), Ansible configures them (its strength — idempotent plays, convergence on every run, drift correction). The provisioners get deleted; the playbook becomes the configuration source of truth; the pipeline runs terraform apply → ansible-playbook. The correction is the division of labor the tools were designed for — each doing what the other can't.
More provisioners, better written.
Configure servers manually.
200 servers is too many.
scenarios.hint: 200 servers configured via provisioners: drift rampant, reruns no-op — what is the correction?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It reassigns each tool to its strength, deletes the anti-pattern, and describes the pipeline — the division of labor applied. B/C/D keep or worsen.

scenarios.title: The Stale Fleet
scenarios.situation: The static inventory lists 80 hosts; 30 were terminated months ago. A security playbook runs 'successfully' — against 50 live hosts and 30 dead ones, with the failures ignored. The team believes all 80 are patched.
evidence: 80 listed, 30 dead; playbook 'succeeds'; team believes all patched.
choices: Dynamic inventory (aws_ec2 plugin or Terraform-constructed — the inventory reflects the actual fleet, dead hosts vanish automatically) AND failure handling (unreachable hosts must fail the play, not log-and-continue — `any_errors_fatal` or max_fail_percentage). The incident had two gaps: the inventory lied (stale) and the playbook didn't care (failures ignored). Truthful inventory + honest failure = the patching you think you have.
Update the static file manually each time.
The 30 dead hosts don't matter.
Ignore unreachable hosts.
scenarios.hint: A stale inventory + ignored failures fake a successful patch run — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It fixes both gaps (dynamic inventory for truth, failure handling for honesty) and states the compound principle — the patching you think you have versus what you have. B ritualizes; C/D deny.

scenarios.title: The Cascading Restart
scenarios.situation: A playbook restarts the app service on EVERY run (the task always reports 'changed'). Rolling across 200 hosts, every deploy causes a full-fleet restart storm — brief outages each time, even when nothing changed.
evidence: task always 'changed'; 200-host rolling restart storm per deploy.
choices: The task isn't actually idempotent — it reports changed unconditionally (a raw `command: systemctl restart` instead of the `service` module, or a template without change detection). The fix: make the task convergent (use the service/template modules — they detect state), notify the handler ONLY on real change, and verify with the run-twice test (second run: zero changes). The restart storm was the playbook lying about 'changed' — idempotence is the contract, and this task broke it.
Restarts are normal; accept the storm.
Deploy less often.
Restart manually instead.
scenarios.hint: Every playbook run restarts all 200 hosts even with no changes — what is the failure?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It identifies the mechanism (unconditional 'changed' — wrong module or missing detection), gives the convergent fix (proper modules + handler notification), and the verification (run-twice test). B/C/D accept or avoid.

scenarios.title: The Committed Password File
scenarios.situation: The `.vault_password` file is committed to the repo ('for CI convenience'). Every secret in the repo is now decryptable by anyone with read access — the encryption is theater.
objectives: Secrets via secret store, never repo
evidence: .vault_password committed 'for CI convenience'; all secrets decryptable.
choices: Remove the file from git (and history — it's compromised), rekey all vault content (`ansible-vault rekey` — the old password is burned), and move the password to CI secret storage (GitHub Actions secrets, etc. — injected as ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE at runtime, never in the repo). The convenience that destroyed the security model gets replaced by the proper channel: secrets flow through the secret store, not the repo. And rotate anything the old password protected.
It's fine; the repo is private.
Rename the file to hide it.
Vault is broken.
scenarios.hint: The vault password file is committed to git — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It treats the password as burned (rekey everything, purge history), gives the proper channel (CI secret store → runtime env), and mandates rotation — the full incident response. B/C/D deny or hide.

scenarios.title: The Mystery Run
scenarios.situation: Someone ran the production playbook from their laptop with extra-vars from a chat message. The change worked — but nobody knows exactly what ran, with which variables, or who approved it. The next incident can't reconstruct it.
objectives: Map each gap to its fix
evidence: laptop run with chat extra-vars; worked; unreconstructable.
choices: The audit and control gaps: job templates (the playbook + its sanctioned parameters — no chat-message extra-vars), RBAC (only authorized roles launch prod jobs), credentials vaulted and injected (no local secrets), and the recorded run (who launched, which template, which parameters, full output — the reconstruction the incident needs). The laptop run was ungoverned automation; AWX makes it governed — same Ansible, with the control plane the organization requires.
Ban laptop Ansible.
The change worked; move on.
Document runs manually.
scenarios.hint: An untracked laptop playbook run can't be reconstructed — what does AWX fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It maps each gap to the AWX fix (templates, RBAC, vaulted credentials, recorded runs) and frames the graduation (same Ansible, governed). B bans without replacing; C/D accept the gap.

scenarios.title: The Half-Applied Pipeline
scenarios.situation: The pipeline's Terraform stage succeeds (50 instances up); the Ansible stage fails (bad variable). The pipeline stops — leaving 50 unconfigured instances. There's no documented failure policy; the team argues for an hour about retry vs rollback while the broken fleet sits.
evidence: TF ok (50 up), Ansible failed; no policy; 1-hr argument; fleet sits broken.
choices: The failure policy, decided in advance: the pipeline design should state per-stage failure handling (Ansible failure → retry N times (idempotent, safe) → then the rollback/escalation decision with the blast-radius criteria). The hour-long argument during the incident is the missing policy's cost — and the unconfigured fleet sitting is the missing auto-response (quarantine the instances: remove from load balancer, mark tainted). Design the failure paths with the same care as the success paths.
The pipeline should never fail.
Retry until it works.
Always roll back.
scenarios.hint: Terraform succeeds, Ansible fails, no failure policy — an hour of argument — what was missing?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the missing artifact (the pre-decided failure policy), gives its content (retry-then-decide with criteria), and the auto-response (quarantine) — failure paths designed like success paths. B/C/D absolutize.

domains.name: Packer Image Pipelines
domains.description: Immutable infrastructure: Packer builders, provisioners, and the golden-image pipeline.

scenarios.title: The Snowflake AMI
scenarios.situation: The 'golden AMI' was built by hand 8 months ago (console clicks + SSH). Nobody knows what's in it; rebuilding is impossible; a CVE in its OpenSSL can't be patched without starting over by hand.
evidence: 8-month-old hand-built AMI; contents unknown; CVE unpatchable.
choices: Codify the image as a Packer template: the base AMI filter, the provisioners (the Ansible playbook — the configuration as code), the timestamped naming — the entire image definition in git, rebuildable with one command. The CVE patch becomes: update the playbook/base filter, `packer build`, test the new image, promote. The snowflake (unique, unreproducible) becomes cattle (versioned, rebuildable) — the immutable pattern replacing archaeology.
Document the hand-built steps.
SSH in and patch OpenSSL.
The AMI is fine; leave it.
scenarios.hint: A hand-built golden AMI can't be rebuilt or patched — what is the correction?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives the codification (template in git, rebuildable), the new CVE workflow (update → build → test → promote), and the snowflake-to-cattle framing. B/C preserve the archaeology; D denies.

scenarios.title: The Leaking Image
scenarios.situation: A built AMI contains the build-time AWS credentials (in shell history), the Jenkins workspace path (in logs), and the test private key (in /tmp). Every instance launched from it carries the residue.
evidence: AMI contains build creds (history), paths (logs), test key (/tmp).
choices: The cleanup provisioner as mandatory final step (history shredded, logs cleared, temp purged, host keys removed) AND the deeper fix: no secrets in provisioners at all (credentials via instance profile/role — never in inline scripts; the residue problem is the symptom, secret-in-build is the disease). The leaked AMI gets deprecated (never deleted while instances run — mark deprecated, migrate, then deregister). Cleanup + secret-hygiene, the image pipeline's non-negotiables.
Delete the AMI.
The residue is harmless.
Manually clean one instance.
scenarios.hint: A built AMI leaks credentials, paths, and keys in every instance — what is the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gives both layers (cleanup provisioner + no-secrets-in-build), the AMI deprecation sequence (not deletion), and names the non-negotiables. B/C/D underreact or misunderstand.

scenarios.title: The CVE AMI
scenarios.situation: A promoted AMI contains a critical OpenSSL CVE. It's already deployed to 300 instances. The image was never scanned — 'the base AMI is from Amazon, it's fine.'
evidence: critical OpenSSL CVE in promoted AMI; 300 instances; never scanned.
scenarios.prompt: What is the response and the prevention?
choices: Response: build the patched image (updated base/provisioner), scan it clean, promote through the pipeline, and roll the fleet (the immutable pattern's strength — the rollout is an image swap, fast and atomic). Prevention: Trivy/Grype scan EVERY build as a pipeline gate (the base layer is still software — 'from Amazon' isn't a CVE exemption), with critical CVEs blocking promotion. The scan gate makes this class of incident structurally rare.
SSH into 300 instances and patch.
Amazon's AMIs are safe.
The CVE is theoretical.
scenarios.hint: A promoted AMI ships a critical CVE to 300 instances — what is the response?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It uses the immutable pattern's strength (image-swap rollout) for the response and installs the scan gate for prevention — with the base-layer reality check. B is the mutable regression; C/D deny.

scenarios.title: The SID Collision
scenarios.situation: Fifty Windows instances from an un-Sysprepped image join the domain — with duplicate SIDs. Domain joins fail mysteriously, group policies apply erratically, and the helpdesk drowns.
evidence: 50 instances, duplicate SIDs, failing joins; image never Sysprepped.
choices: Sysprep generalization (`/generalize` — the SID reset, the one-shot specialization): without it, every instance is the same machine identity — the domain sees fifty clones of one computer. The fix: Sysprep in the Packer build (the powershell provisioner, `only` the Windows source), rebuild the image, redeploy. And the process fix: the image test asserts generalization (the InSpec control checking for the Sysprep marker). Skipped generalization is the Windows-image original sin.
The domain is broken.
Fifty instances is too many.
Join the domain manually.
scenarios.hint: Fifty Windows instances with duplicate SIDs break domain joins — what was skipped?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It names the skipped step precisely (Sysprep /generalize), explains the mechanism (duplicate machine identity), gives the build fix + test, and the process addition. B/C/D misdiagnose.

scenarios.title: The Stale Fleet
scenarios.situation: The fleet runs 14-month-old AMIs. Three critical CVEs are unpatched. The image pipeline exists — but nobody has triggered a build in a year ('nothing changed').
evidence: fleet on 14-month AMIs; 3 critical CVEs; pipeline idle 1 year.
choices: Scheduled rebuilds: the pipeline runs on cron (weekly/monthly) regardless of 'changes' — because base images accumulate CVEs and the playbooks evolve, 'nothing changed' is never true for 14 months. The schedule makes freshness structural, not remembered. Plus the scan gate (blocking promotion on critical CVEs) and the fleet-roll automation (the new image flows to launch templates → rolling replacement). The stale fleet is the unscheduled pipeline's predictable output.
Rebuild when CVEs are announced.
The old AMIs are fine.
Patch instances in place.
scenarios.hint: 14-month-old AMIs with unpatched CVEs; pipeline exists but never triggered — what is the fix?

lessons.title: GitOps — Core concepts
concepts: GitOps makes git the single source of truth: desired state is declared in version control, and an in-cluster agent (ArgoCD, Flux) continuously reconciles live state toward it.
Reconciliation is a loop — observe, diff, sync: drift between git and cluster is detected automatically and either corrected (auto-sync) or surfaced for approval (manual sync).
Pull-based delivery beats push-based: the agent inside the cluster pulls changes, so CI never needs cluster credentials — a major reduction in secret sprawl.
The app-of-apps pattern composes Applications hierarchically, giving each team its own sync scope, policies, and blast radius instead of one giant sync.
Secrets don't belong in git — store references (ExternalSecrets, Vault Agent) and let the cluster resolve real values from a secrets manager at runtime.
Immutable image references (digests or version tags) keep git honest: with mutable tags like 'latest', the repo stops describing what's actually running.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/gitops.git
    path: apps/web
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: web
example.walkthrough: This ArgoCD Application points at the apps/web directory of the gitops repo on main and the web namespace in-cluster. The agent continuously compares the two and syncs differences according to the sync policy.

pitfalls: Common trap: committing Secrets with base64 'encryption' — base64 is encoding; use external secret references.
Common trap: using ':latest' image tags — the repo stops describing reality and rollbacks become impossible.
Common trap: one Application syncing everything — a bad commit has unlimited blast radius; use app-of-apps.
Common trap: CI pushing directly to the cluster alongside GitOps — two writers fight; let the agent be the only writer.

lessons.title: HCL Syntax & Resource Blocks
concepts: HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) is the declarative DSL Terraform evaluates: blocks (resource, variable, output) with labels and a body of arguments. Unlike YAML, HCL is purpose-built for configuration — it has first-class expressions, comments, and heredocs, and `terraform fmt` enforces canonical style. The resource block is the atom: `resource "aws_instance" "web" { ... }` declares desired state, and Terraform's provider plugin turns it into API calls.

Every resource block has a type (the provider's resource, e.g. `aws_instance`) and a local name (your handle for references: `aws_instance.web.id`). Arguments map to the provider schema — required vs optional is defined per resource, and `terraform validate` catches schema errors before any API call. The distinction between the resource TYPE (what it is in the provider) and NAME (what you call it) is the foundation of every reference expression.

Providers are plugins Terraform downloads during `terraform init` — the `required_providers` block pins source and version (`hashicorp/aws ~> 5.0`). Version constraints matter enormously: an unpinned provider can introduce breaking schema changes on the next init. The lock file (`.terraform.lock.hcl`) records exact versions — commit it.

The evaluation order: Terraform parses all `.tf` files in a directory as one configuration (file boundaries don't matter), builds a dependency graph from references, then plans. This is why splitting files is organizational only — `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf` are conventions, and references work across files freely.

example.walkthrough: The configuration declares the provider pin, one EC2 instance resource, and an output. Note the three block types (terraform, resource, output), the resource's type/name pair (`aws_instance`/`web`), the variable interpolation in tags, and the output's reference expression (`aws_instance.web.public_ip`) — the cross-block reference that builds the dependency graph. `terraform fmt` would canonicalize the alignment; the lock file pins the exact provider build.

pitfalls: Unpinned providers: `version = ">= 0"` (or absent) lets the next init pull breaking schema changes — pin with `~>`.
File-boundary thinking: splitting resources across files changes nothing semantically — don't 'fix' reference errors by moving blocks between files.
Forgetting the lock file: `.terraform.lock.hcl` uncommitted means teammates get different provider builds — commit it.
lessons.try_it: Write a config declaring an S3 bucket with versioning enabled, a pinned AWS provider, and an output for the bucket ARN. Run terraform fmt and terraform validate.

lessons.title: Variables, Locals & Outputs
concepts: Input variables (`variable` blocks) are the configuration's API: `type` constraints (string, number, bool, list(string), map, object, tuple), `default` values, `description`, `validation` rules, and `sensitive = true` for secrets. Variables are set via `-var`, `-var-file`, `*.auto.tfvars`, or environment (`TF_VAR_name`) — with a clear precedence order. Required variables (no default) fail the plan if unset, which is the mechanism for mandatory inputs.

Locals (`locals` blocks) are internal named expressions — computed values reused across the config (common tags, derived names). Unlike variables, locals can't be set from outside; they're the DRY mechanism for derived values. The rule of thumb: variables for inputs, locals for computations — and when a value is computed from variables, it belongs in locals, not repeated inline.

Outputs expose values: to the user after apply, to other configurations via `terraform_remote_state`, and to modules' callers. `sensitive = true` on outputs redacts them from CLI output — but they're still in the state file in plaintext, so sensitive outputs are not a security mechanism, just display hygiene.

Validation blocks (`validation { condition = ... error_message = ... }`) turn runtime surprises into plan-time errors: `condition = contains(["dev","prod"], var.environment)`. Combined with precise `object()` types, validation makes misconfiguration fail fast with clear messages — the cheapest error is the one caught at plan.

example.walkthrough: The variable block shows the full API surface: type constraint, description, and a validation rule that fails the plan on bad input. The sensitive variable demonstrates secret handling (redacted display, still plaintext in state). Locals derive the reusable values (common tags, computed DB name) — the DRY mechanism. The sensitive output shows display hygiene. Together: variables for inputs, locals for computations, outputs for exposure.

pitfalls: Sensitive as security: `sensitive = true` only redacts CLI display — the value is plaintext in state; use a secrets manager for real secrecy.
Validation-free variables: without validation blocks, typos become 4 AM apply failures — validate at the boundary.
Inline repetition: computing the same derived value in five resources instead of one locals block — the DRY violation.
lessons.try_it: Add a validated `region` variable (must match `^[a-z]{2}-[a-z]+-[0-9]$`), a locals block deriving three tagged names, and a sensitive output. Test with a bad region value.

lessons.title: Expressions, Functions & For-Each
concepts: HCL expressions turn static config into computed infrastructure: conditionals (`var.ha ? 3 : 1`), string directives (`%{ for }` templates), and 100+ built-in functions (`cidrsubnet`, `merge`, `jsonencode`, `try`, `coalesce`). The `terraform console` command is the REPL for experimenting — every expression can be tested before it's committed to config.

The `for` expression transforms collections: `[for s in var.subnets : s.id]` or `{for k, v in var.tags : k => upper(v)}`. Combined with `...` (ellipsis) grouping, for-expressions reshape data between modules. They're the primary tool for adapting one module's outputs to another's inputs.

Meta-arguments multiply resources: `count` (N identical instances, indexed by `count.index`) vs `for_each` (one instance per map key/set element, addressed by `each.key`/`each.value`). The critical difference: `count` addresses by position (removing item 0 renumbers everything — destructive), `for_each` addresses by key (removing one key only destroys that instance). For anything with identity, `for_each` wins.

`dynamic` blocks generate nested blocks programmatically (`dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.ports ... }`) — the escape hatch when a resource needs a variable number of nested blocks. And `lifecycle` customizes behavior: `create_before_destroy`, `prevent_destroy`, `ignore_changes` — the fine print that prevents outages.

example.walkthrough: The three multiplication patterns side by side: for_each with a set (each member keyed by name — removing 'alice' destroys only alice), count with positional indexing (removing index 0 cascades — the classic footgun), and dynamic blocks generating ingress rules from a variable port list. The comments flag the identity semantics, which is the decision criterion: identity → for_each, fungible replicas → count.

pitfalls: count for named things: using count for users/buckets/DNS records means one removal renumbers and recreates — for_each for identity.
for_each over a list: lists have no stable keys — convert with toset() or a map, or face the 'keys must be known' error.
dynamic overuse: dynamic blocks for static content hurt readability — use them only when the count genuinely varies.
lessons.try_it: Build a config creating one S3 bucket per team (for_each over a map of team→purpose), with dynamic lifecycle rules. Remove one team and verify only its bucket is destroyed (plan).

lessons.title: Dependency Graph & Lifecycle Rules
concepts: Terraform builds a DAG from references: `aws_instance.web` referenced by `aws_eip.web` means the instance precedes the EIP. Implicit dependencies (via references) are preferred — the graph is derived, not declared. `depends_on` (explicit) is the escape hatch for hidden dependencies (an API call ordering the provider can't see), and overuse signals a design smell.

`lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` reverses the default destroy-then-create for replacements — essential for resources that can't have downtime (launch templates, security groups referenced elsewhere). Without it, replacing a security group destroys it first, detaching all instances momentarily.

`lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` makes destroy plans fail — the guardrail for databases, state buckets, production VPCs. It's the cheapest insurance against the 3 AM `terraform destroy` catastrophe. `ignore_changes` tells Terraform to stop managing specific arguments (e.g., `tags` managed by another tool, or `desired_count` managed by autoscaling).

`terraform graph | dot` renders the DAG — the debugging tool when ordering surprises you. And `depends_on` in outputs/modules propagates ordering. The mental model: Terraform is a graph walker, not a script runner — ordering emerges from the graph, and lifecycle blocks tune the walker's behavior at the edges.

example.walkthrough: The lifecycle patterns: create_before_destroy on the launch template (replacement without downtime — the new template exists before the old is destroyed), prevent_destroy on the production database (destroy plans fail — the 3 AM guardrail), ignore_changes on tags (another tool manages them — stop fighting). The depends_on shows the explicit escape hatch for hidden ordering. Together they're the fine print that separates working config from production-safe config.

pitfalls: depends_on everywhere: explicit dependencies for what references already express — the graph knows; overuse is a smell.
Missing create_before_destroy: replacing launch templates/security groups with default ordering causes momentary detachment — downtime by default.
ignore_changes as drift license: ignoring changes you should be managing hides real drift — use it only for externally-managed arguments.
lessons.try_it: Add prevent_destroy to a database resource and run terraform plan -destroy — observe the failure. Then model a launch template replacement with and without create_before_destroy (plan only).

lessons.title: What State Is & Why It Exists
