example.walkthrough: The handoff pattern: Terraform's JSON outputs become Ansible's inventory (the contract between the tools), with the playbook converging the software layer. The commented local-exec shows the single legitimate provisioner use — pure data plumbing (writing the inventory file), not configuration. The WHAT/HOW split is the mental model: Terraform the platform, Ansible the machine.

pitfalls: Provisioners for config: the last-resort lesson — remote-exec installing packages is Ansible's job (convergence, drift, reruns).
Ansible for lifecycle: cloud modules without state — provisioning in Ansible is imperative; lifecycle belongs to Terraform.
Manual handoff: copy-pasting IPs from Terraform output into the inventory — the dynamic inventory is the contract.
lessons.try_it: Build the handoff: Terraform creates 2 instances with outputs, a script generates the Ansible inventory from outputs, and a playbook installs nginx. Run the full loop twice (verify idempotence).

lessons.title: Inventory: Static, Dynamic & Patterns
concepts: Static inventory (the INI/YAML file): groups, hosts, group_vars/host_vars — the simple, reviewable, git-versioned starting point. `[web]`, `[db]`, children groups (`[prod:children]`), and the variable precedence (all → group → host). For stable infrastructure, static inventory is honest and sufficient.

Dynamic inventory (the cloud plugins): `aws_ec2` inventory plugin querying the API at runtime — hosts by tags, groups by attributes (`keyed_groups`), compose variables from instance metadata. The inventory is always current (no stale IPs), at the cost of API dependence and the compose-variable learning curve.

The Terraform-sourced inventory: the constructed plugin reading `terraform output -json` (or the state directly) — the handoff made native. Groups from output structures, hostvars from attributes. This is the tightest integration: the inventory IS the Terraform outputs, no duplication.

Patterns: group_vars per environment (dev/staging/prod), `limit` for blast-radius control (`--limit web[0]` — the canary), and the inventory as documentation (groups named by role, variables showing intent). The inventory describes the fleet's structure — keep it truthful.

example.code:
# Dynamic inventory: aws_ec2 plugin (always current)
# inventory.aws_ec2.yml
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions:
  - us-east-1
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: role
  - key: tags.Environment
    prefix: env
compose:
  ansible_host: public_ip_address

# ansible-inventory -i inventory.aws_ec2.yml --graph
# @role_web:
#   |-- i-0abcd (ansible_host=54.1.2.3)
# @env_prod:
#   |-- i-0abcd
example.walkthrough: The aws_ec2 dynamic inventory: hosts discovered from the API at runtime, grouped by tags (role_web, env_prod), ansible_host composed from the public IP. The --graph output shows the group structure. No stale IPs, no manual file — the inventory reflects the actual fleet. The static-vs-dynamic decision (stable→static, fluid→dynamic) and the Terraform-constructed option complete the picture.

pitfalls: Stale static inventory: the INI file from 6 months ago — half the hosts dead; dynamic or generated for fluid fleets.
No limit discipline: running the playbook against all 500 hosts at once — --limit for canaries, always.
Inventory as secrets: passwords in group_vars plaintext — Ansible Vault (next topic) or the secret stays out.
lessons.try_it: Build both: a static inventory for 3 test hosts and a dynamic aws_ec2 inventory (or the constructed Terraform variant). Compare ansible-inventory --graph outputs.

lessons.title: Roles, Playbooks & Idempotence
concepts: Roles are the unit of reuse: `roles/nginx/{tasks,handlers,templates,files,vars,defaults,meta}` — the directory convention Ansible Galaxy and every team expects. Tasks declare desired state (`package: name=nginx state=present`), handlers react to change (restart on config change — notified, run once at the end), templates render config (Jinja2 — the `template` module).

Idempotence is the contract: running the playbook twice changes nothing the second time (the `creates:` guard, the `changed_when` tuning, the package module's inherent idempotence). Every task should be safe to rerun — the playbook is a convergent loop, not a script. Test it: run twice, assert zero changes on the second.

The play structure: plays map hosts to roles (`hosts: web`, `roles: [nginx, app]`), with `become` for privilege, `serial` for rolling execution (the canary: `serial: 1` then `serial: "25%"`), and `max_fail_percentage` for the abort threshold. The playbook is the orchestration; the roles are the units.

Galaxy and requirements: `requirements.yml` pins role versions (the dependency discipline, again) — `ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml` in CI. And `ansible-lint` in CI (the fmt/validate/tflint of the Ansible world) — the hygiene pipeline both tools deserve.

example.code:
# roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml: idempotent, handler-notified
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Render nginx config
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: Reload nginx

# roles/nginx/handlers/main.yml
- name: Reload nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: reloaded

# site.yml: the orchestration
- hosts: web
  become: true
  serial: "25%"
  max_fail_percentage: 25
  roles: [nginx, app]
example.walkthrough: The role anatomy: idempotent tasks (package present, template rendered), the handler (reload notified only on config change — run once at the end), and the play (rolling 25% serial, 25% max-fail abort, become for privilege). The run-twice-zero-changes test is the idempotence proof. Galaxy requirements + ansible-lint give the dependency and hygiene discipline.

pitfalls: Non-idempotent tasks: the shell/command without creates:/changed_when — reruns redo work or fail; every task rerunnable.
Handler spam: notify on every task — handlers run once at the end, but only notify on actual change.
Unpinned Galaxy roles: floating role versions — requirements.yml pins, CI installs.
lessons.try_it: Write an nginx role (tasks, handlers, templates). Run the playbook twice against a test host; assert zero changes on the second run. Add ansible-lint to CI.

lessons.title: Ansible Vault & Secrets
concepts: Ansible Vault encrypts secrets in git: `ansible-vault encrypt_string` for inline values, `encrypt` for files, vault IDs for multiple environments (`--vault-id dev@prompt`). The encrypted strings live in group_vars/host_vars — versioned, reviewable, decryptable only with the password. The 'Secrets in the GitOps repo' problem, Ansible edition.

The password management: vault passwords in CI via environment/secret store (never in the repo — the `.vault_pass` file committed is the classic self-own), per-environment vault IDs (dev/prod keys separated — the blast radius), and rotation (rekey with `ansible-vault rekey` — the password change without re-encrypting everything by hand).

The better pattern: no long-lived secrets at all — the lookup plugins (`amazon.aws.aws_secret`, `community.hashi_vault.vault_kv2_get`) fetch at runtime from the secrets manager. Vault-encrypted statics are the fallback; dynamic lookups are the standard. The hierarchy: dynamic > vault-encrypted > (never) plaintext.

The `no_log: true` task attribute (suppress secret values in output — the display hygiene) and the CI masking complete the picture. Secrets appear in exactly three places: the manager, the encrypted file, the runtime memory — never logs, never git plaintext, never chat.

example.code:
# group_vars/prod/vault.yml (encrypted at rest in git)
# $ ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cr3t!' --name 'db_password'
# db_password: !vault |
#   $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
#   623265...encrypted...

# Prefer: runtime lookup (no stored secret at all)
- name: Get DB password at runtime
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    db_password: "{{ lookup('amazon.aws.aws_secret', 'prod/db/password') }}"
  no_log: true   # never in output
example.walkthrough: The two patterns: vault-encrypted inline strings (AES256 in git, decrypted with the vault password — the fallback) and the preferred runtime lookup (fetched from the secrets manager at execution, never stored — with no_log suppressing output). The hierarchy (dynamic > vault > never plaintext) and the password-management discipline (CI via secret store, per-env IDs, rekey for rotation) complete the secrets story.

pitfalls: Committed vault password: the .vault_pass in git decrypts everything — the self-own; CI via secret store.
Single vault ID: one password for dev and prod — per-environment IDs (blast radius).
Logged secrets: the debug task printing the password — no_log: true, always, on secret tasks.
lessons.try_it: Encrypt a string with ansible-vault, use it in a playbook, and run with --vault-id. Then convert one secret to a runtime lookup (mock the secrets manager if needed).

lessons.title: The CI Pipeline: Terraform → Ansible in Automation
concepts: The automated handoff: CI runs Terraform apply (the platform converges), generates the inventory from outputs (the contract, scripted), runs the Ansible playbook (the configuration converges), then verifies (the smoke tests — the loop's proof). Four stages, one pipeline, the two tools orchestrated — the division of labor, automated.

State passing between stages: Terraform outputs as pipeline artifacts (the JSON artifact the inventory script reads), the state backend as the shared memory (both stages read the same remote state), and the run ID tagging (every resource tagged with the pipeline run — the audit trail of which automation created what).

Failure handling: Terraform failure stops the pipeline (no inventory, no configure — the platform isn't ready); Ansible failure triggers the decision (retry? the playbook is idempotent — or roll back the Terraform apply? the blast-radius call). The pipeline needs the failure policy documented BEFORE the 3 AM page — not invented during it.

The scheduling dimension: one-shot pipelines (the change-driven run) vs scheduled convergence (the nightly ansible-playbook against the dynamic inventory — the configuration drift correction, Terraform's refresh-only equivalent for the machine layer). Both belong in the platform: change-driven for deploys, scheduled for hygiene.

example.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml: the orchestrated handoff
# stages: [provision, inventory, configure, verify]
# provision:
#   script: terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan
#   artifacts: { paths: [tf-outputs.json] }   # the contract
# inventory:
#   script: ./scripts/gen-inventory.py tf-outputs.json > inventory.ini
#   artifacts: { paths: [inventory.ini] }
# configure:
#   script: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml
#   # failure here: retry (idempotent) or rollback decision
# verify:
#   script: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh   # the loop's proof
example.walkthrough: The four-stage pipeline: provision (Terraform, outputs as artifacts), inventory (the contract generated), configure (Ansible, idempotent), verify (smoke tests — the proof). The failure policy per stage (stop vs retry-vs-rollback decision) and the scheduling dimension (change-driven + nightly hygiene) complete the automation picture. The artifacts chain is the state passing.

pitfalls: Undocumented failure policy: the 3 AM 'do we retry or roll back?' — decided in the pipeline design, not the incident.
Manual inventory between stages: the human copying outputs — the generation script is the contract; automate it.
No scheduled convergence: change-driven only — the nightly Ansible run is the machine layer's drift correction.
lessons.try_it: Build the 4-stage pipeline (or simulate with scripts): provision → inventory → configure → verify. Then break the configure stage deliberately and execute your failure policy.

lessons.title: Builders & the Immutable Pattern
concepts: Packer's builders create machine images: `amazon-ebs` (EC2 AMIs), `docker`, `vsphere-iso`, `googlecompute`, `azure-arm` — each builder knows its platform's image API. The template declares `sources` (which builders) and `build` (what to do) — one definition, many platforms (the AMI and the Docker image from the same provisioners).

The immutable pattern: bake the configuration INTO the image (packages, files, services — at build time), then deploy the image unchanged (no SSH, no post-deploy config). Contrast the mutable pattern (deploy base image, configure after — the configuration drift the immutable pattern eliminates). Immutable: the artifact is the configuration, versioned and tested as a unit.

The build block: `sources` (builders to run), `provisioners` (shell/ansible/puppet — the configuration, run at build time in a sandbox), `post-processors` (manifest, compress, upload — the artifact handling). `packer build template.pkr.hcl` runs the whole pipeline — and `packer validate`/`fmt` give the familiar hygiene.

Why immutable wins at scale: deployment becomes image swap (fast, atomic, rollback = previous image), configuration drift becomes impossible (nobody SSHes to 'fix' the image — they build a new one), and testing shifts left (the image is tested before any deployment). The pets-vs-cattle line, implemented.

example.walkthrough: The Packer template: plugin pinning (the dependency discipline, again), the amazon-ebs source (filtered base AMI, timestamped name — every build versioned), and the build block running the Ansible playbook as the provisioner (the SAME playbook from the Ansible domain — one configuration definition, baked at build time). The provisioner here is correct usage: build-time in a sandbox, not deploy-time on live servers.

pitfalls: Mutable habits: SSHing into 'fix' the golden image — the image is immutable; build a new one.
Unversioned AMIs: ami_name without timestamp/version — unidentifiable artifacts; every build named and tracked.
Unpinned plugins: floating builder plugins — required_plugins pins, like providers.
lessons.try_it: Write a Packer template (amazon-ebs or docker builder) that provisions with your Ansible nginx role. Build it, verify the image, and note the build time.

lessons.title: Provisioners at Build Time
concepts: Packer provisioners run during the BUILD (in the sandbox instance/container) — this is their correct habitat, unlike Terraform's deploy-time provisioners. The `shell` provisioner (inline scripts, ordered), `ansible` (the playbook — reusing the Ansible domain's roles), `file` (uploading assets), `powershell`/`windows-shell` for Windows images.

The ordering: provisioners run in sequence — base setup (shell: updates, base packages) → configuration (ansible: the roles) → hardening (shell: CIS benchmarks, cleanup) → validation (inspec/serverspec: the image tests). Each layer's output is the next layer's input; the sequence is the recipe.

The cleanup provisioner (the last one): remove SSH host keys, clear logs, zero free space (`dd if=/dev/zero`), remove the build user — the image that ships contains no build residue. Uncleaned images leak the build environment (keys, history, temp files) into every deployment.

Idempotence at build time matters less (the sandbox is fresh each build) but the provisioners should still be the SAME convergent code as deploy-time config (the Ansible roles reused) — one definition of 'configured,' used at build. The DRY across the pipeline.

example.walkthrough: The provisioner sequence: base setup (shell), configuration (the shared Ansible playbook — same roles as the Ansible domain), cleanup (logs, history, temp — no build residue ships). The ordering is the recipe; the Ansible reuse is the DRY across build and deploy. Packer provisioners are correct here because they run at build time in a disposable sandbox — the opposite of Terraform's deploy-time anti-pattern.

pitfalls: Build residue: shipping the image with host keys, logs, history — the cleanup provisioner is mandatory.
Divergent config: build-time shell scripts duplicating the Ansible roles — one definition (the roles), used at build.
Secrets in provisioners: credentials in inline scripts land in the image and the build logs — runtime injection only.
lessons.try_it: Add a cleanup provisioner to your template (logs, history, temp, host keys). Build and verify the residue is gone (launch, inspect).

lessons.title: Image Testing & Promotion
concepts: Test the image, not the deployment: InSpec/serverspec profiles (the CIS benchmark checks, the 'nginx is installed and running' assertions) run against the built image BEFORE promotion — the shift-left for infrastructure. A failing image never becomes a deployment candidate.

The promotion pipeline: build (Packer) → test (InSpec) → scan (Trivy/Grype for CVEs — the image's software inventory checked) → sign (cosign — the supply-chain signature) → promote (copy to prod account/region, mark as latest-stable). Each gate is automated; each artifact is traceable (the manifest post-processor records the build).

The manifest post-processor (`manifest`: writes build artifacts + IDs to JSON) feeds the promotion automation — the pipeline reads the manifest to know WHAT was built (AMI ID, region) without parsing logs. And the `artifice`/`compress` post-processors handle the artifact logistics.

Deprecation and lifecycle: old AMIs get deprecated (not deleted — running instances need them), then deregistered after the migration window, with the EBS snapshots cleaned. The AMI lifecycle is the release management of infrastructure — versions, promotion, deprecation, retirement.

example.code:
# The image pipeline (each gate automated, each artifact traced)
#
#   packer build  ->  inspec exec (CIS + app checks)
#     -> trivy image (CVE scan)  ->  cosign sign (supply chain)
#       -> manifest.json (what was built: AMI IDs, regions)
#         -> promote (copy to prod, mark stable)
#           -> deprecate old (not delete)  ->  deregister + cleanup
#
# A failing image never becomes a deployment candidate.
example.walkthrough: The pipeline diagram (build → test → scan → sign → promote → deprecate) with each gate's purpose: InSpec for configuration correctness, Trivy for CVEs, cosign for supply-chain, manifest for traceability. The deprecate-not-delete discipline and the 'failing image never deploys' principle make it the release management of infrastructure.

pitfalls: Untested images: the AMI that 'built fine' — build success isn't correctness; InSpec asserts it.
Unscanned images: the CVE that ships in the base layer — Trivy/Grype at build time, every build.
Deleted old AMIs: deregistering while instances still run — deprecate, migrate, then clean.
lessons.try_it: Write an InSpec profile (5 controls: package installed, service running, port listening, file content, no default creds). Run it against your built image.

lessons.title: HCP Packer: Channels & Image Metadata
concepts: HCP Packer is the image registry: Packer pushes build metadata (the iteration — what was built, when, from which template) to the HCP bucket; channels (dev/staging/prod) point at iterations (the promotion pointers — 'prod' means THIS iteration). The registry answers 'which image is prod on?' without tribal knowledge.

The promotion workflow: build → iteration created → test gates (the InSpec/Trivy results recorded against the iteration) → channel assignment (staging channel → prod channel — the promotion as a pointer move, auditable). Rollback is channel reassignment (point prod back — the 30-second rollback).

The Terraform integration: the `hcp_packer_image` data source reads the channel ('give me the prod channel's AMI ID for this bucket') — Terraform always deploys the channel's image, never a hardcoded AMI. The hardcoded-AMI problem (the 'which AMI is current?' spreadsheet) dissolves: the channel is the answer.

The iteration hygiene: retention (old iterations expire — the registry doesn't grow forever), the build fingerprinting (which template commit built it — the traceability), and the multi-region replication (the iteration's AMIs copied per region — the channel resolves per region). The image supply chain, managed.

example.walkthrough: The HCP Packer pattern: the build pushes metadata to the bucket (labeled, described), channels point at iterations (promotion as pointer moves), and Terraform's hcp_packer_image data source reads the production channel — the AMI ID is never hardcoded. Rollback is channel reassignment. The 'which AMI is current' question gets a structural answer.

pitfalls: Hardcoded AMI IDs: the spreadsheet of current AMIs — the channel data source dissolves it.
Channel-less promotion: 'just deploy the newest' — the channel is the deliberate gate; newest isn't prod-ready by default.
Iteration sprawl: no retention — the registry grows forever; expire old iterations.
lessons.try_it: Set up an HCP Packer bucket (free tier) with dev/prod channels. Push a build, assign channels, and read the prod channel from Terraform via the data source.

lessons.title: GitOps Principles: Declarative, Versioned, Pulled, Reconciled
concepts: The four GitOps principles (the OpenGitOps definition): declarative (the desired state is expressed as code — YAML, HCL — not as imperative steps), versioned and immutable (stored in git — every change reviewed, every state recoverable), pulled automatically (agents inside the target pull — not CI pushing in), and continuously reconciled (the agent converges reality to the declared state, forever). Four properties; the whole discipline.

Declarative vs imperative: `kubectl apply -f` of a checked-in manifest is declarative-ish; the `kubectl scale` typed at 2 AM is imperative — and the reconciler's job is erasing the difference (reverting the 2 AM edit). Versioned means the audit trail is the git log (who changed prod = git blame) — the compliance story GitOps tells for free.

Pulled vs pushed: in push, CI holds cluster credentials and applies outward (the credential-sprawl and blast-radius problem); in pull, the agent holds its own credentials and fetches inward (credentials never leave the cluster boundary). The security architecture follows the topology — pull is the zero-trust-aligned shape.

Continuously reconciled: the loop never stops — the agent watches git AND the cluster, converging both directions (git changes apply; cluster drift reverts). This is the property the other three serve: declaration without reconciliation is documentation; versioning without pull is a backup; pull without reconciliation is a delivery mechanism. Reconciliation is the engine.

example.code:
# The four principles (OpenGitOps)
#
#   1. DECLARATIVE: desired state as code (not imperative steps)
#   2. VERSIONED: stored in git (reviewed, recoverable, auditable)
#   3. PULLED: agents inside the target fetch (not CI pushing in)
#   4. RECONCILED: continuous convergence (git -> cluster AND
#      cluster drift -> reverted), forever
#
# The engine: 4. The others serve it.
#   declaration without reconciliation = documentation
#   versioning without pull = backup
#   pull without reconciliation = delivery mechanism
example.walkthrough: The four principles with the OpenGitOps framing, each property explained through its failure mode (imperative 2 AM edits, credential sprawl, documentation-without-reconciliation). The 'reconciliation is the engine' close gives the hierarchy — the other three serve the loop. The existing 'kubectl apply from a laptop' scenario is the pre-principles world this replaces.

pitfalls: GitOps as 'git + kubectl': the four properties are conjunctive — missing pull or reconciliation isn't GitOps, it's CI with git.
Principles as slogans: each principle has a mechanism (revert, blame, credential topology, the loop) — know the mechanism.
Reconciliation as optional: the continuous loop is the engine — without it, the rest is documentation and backup.
lessons.try_it: Assess your current deployment pipeline against the four principles (score 0-2 each). Write 200 words: which principle is weakest, and what's the first fix?

lessons.title: Pull vs Push: Reconciliation Architectures
concepts: Push architecture: the CI/CD system authenticates to every target and applies changes outward. Strengths: simple to reason about, works for targets without agents (the database, the SaaS API), immediate feedback in the pipeline. Weaknesses: credential sprawl (N targets × M pipelines of credentials), no drift correction (the pipeline runs on change, not continuously), blast radius (the CI system is the keys to everything).

Pull architecture: agents in each target authenticate outward to git (read-only deploy keys) and reconcile continuously. Strengths: credential topology (targets hold their own access — nothing to steal in CI), continuous reconciliation (drift self-heals), scalability (add a target = install an agent). Weaknesses: needs the agent footprint, pull latency (the interval), and targets that can run agents (not the SaaS API).

The hybrid reality: pull for Kubernetes (ArgoCD/Flux — the agent-native platform), push for the rest (Terraform from CI for the cloud APIs, the database migrations from the pipeline). The mature platform isn't pull-everywhere — it's pull-where-agents-live, push-where-they-can't, with the GitOps principles applied to both (versioned, reviewed, auditable).

The credential math that decides it: count the credentials. Push: every pipeline × every target (grows multiplicatively, leaks catastrophically). Pull: one read-only deploy key per agent (grows additively, leaks minimally — a stolen key reads git, nothing more). When the CISO asks, show the math.

example.code:
# Credential math: push vs pull
#
#   PUSH: credentials = pipelines x targets
#     5 pipelines x 10 clusters = 50 cluster credentials in CI
#     leak one CI secret -> cluster access (write!)
#
#   PULL: credentials = agents (one read-only deploy key each)
#     10 clusters = 10 read-only git keys (in-cluster)
#     leak one key -> git read access (nothing more)
#
#   Hybrid: pull where agents live (K8s),
#           push where they can't (cloud APIs via Terraform).
example.walkthrough: The push/pull comparison with the credential math (multiplicative vs additive — the CISO-ready argument), the honest strengths/weaknesses of each, and the hybrid reality (pull for K8s, push for cloud APIs). The read-only-deploy-key point (leaked key reads git, nothing more) is the security crux.

pitfalls: Pull purism: the SaaS API and the database can't run agents — push where agents can't live, principled.
Push complacency: 'our CI is secure' — the credential math doesn't care about feelings; count the secrets.
Agentless drift: push targets need their own drift story (Terraform's scheduled plans) — no agent, no free reconciliation.
lessons.try_it: Count your organization's deployment credentials (pipelines × targets). Write 200 words: what does the math say about your architecture?

lessons.title: Progressive Delivery: Canary & Blue-Green
concepts: Progressive delivery is the deployment strategy layer: canary (shift 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic to the new version, analyzing metrics at each step), blue-green (two full environments, switch the router — instant rollback by switching back), and feature flags (the code paths toggled at runtime — orthogonal to both). The principle: limit the blast radius of every release, automatically.

Argo Rollouts (the Kubernetes-native implementation): the Rollout CRD replaces the Deployment, with `steps` (setWeight, pause, analysis) — the canary as declared state, reconciled by the rollouts controller. AnalysisTemplates query Prometheus/Datadog (error rate < 1%, p99 < 500ms) — the automated judge promoting or aborting the rollout.

The GitOps integration: the Rollout manifest lives in git (the desired version), ArgoCD syncs it, the rollouts controller executes the progression — GitOps delivers the intent, progressive delivery executes the strategy. The promotion (full cutover) can even be a git commit (the flag flipped by PR) — the release as a reviewed change.

The metrics discipline: canary without analysis is just slow deployment — the AnalysisTemplate with real SLOs (error budget, latency, business metrics) is what makes it progressive delivery rather than progressive hope. Define the abort criteria BEFORE the rollout, not during the incident.

example.code:
# Argo Rollout: canary as declared state
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis:
            templates: [{ templateName: error-rate }]
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService: { name: web-vsvc }
# AnalysisTemplate: error rate < 1% (the automated judge)
example.walkthrough: The Rollout CRD shows the canary as declared state: traffic weights stepped 10→50→100 with pauses, the analysis gate (error-rate template) between steps, Istio traffic routing. The controller executes the progression; the metrics judge it. The manifest in git means the release strategy is reviewed, versioned, and auditable — progressive delivery inside the GitOps loop.

pitfalls: Canary without analysis: stepped traffic with no metrics gate — progressive hope, not progressive delivery.
Abort criteria during the incident: the SLOs must be defined before the rollout — analysis templates, reviewed.
Big-bang by default: the Deployment's rolling update isn't progressive delivery — the strategy needs the Rollout CRD.
lessons.try_it: Deploy an Argo Rollout canary (or simulate with weight steps) with an AnalysisTemplate on error rate. Trigger a failing version and watch the automatic abort + rollback.

lessons.title: ArgoCD Architecture: Server, Controller & Repo Server
concepts: The three core components: `argocd-server` (API + UI — the human interface, stateless), `application-controller` (the reconciliation engine — compares git vs cluster, syncs; the workhorse), `repo-server` (clones git, renders manifests — Helm/Kustomize/plugin execution; the CPU-heavy one). Plus Redis (cache + locks) and Dex (SSO). Each scales independently — the architecture is the scaling guide.

The controller's loop: refresh (every 3m default, or webhook-triggered) → diff (git-rendered vs live, with ignoreDifferences applied) → sync (if automated and out-of-sync) → health assessment (per-resource health.lua). The `--reconciliation-timeout`, `--status-processors`, and sharding (`--shard`) tune it: more clusters/apps = more controller replicas with consistent-hash sharding.

The repo-server's load: every refresh re-renders every app's manifests (Helm template runs, Kustomize builds) — the CPU bottleneck at scale. Symptoms: slow UI diffs, refresh timeouts, OOMKills. Fixes: webhook-triggered refresh (instead of 3m polling), manifest caching, repo-server replicas, and the `helm.valuesFileSchemes` for remote values.

High availability: controller (active-active with sharding — or single with leader election pre-sharding), server (stateless, replicate freely), repo-server (replicate, the cache is in Redis), Redis (HA or the bundled HA mode). The production ArgoCD is a small distributed system — engineer it like one (PDBs, resources, monitoring the workqueue depth).

example.code:
# ArgoCD component map (what scales, what breaks)
#
#   argocd-server        API + UI (stateless) ......... scale freely
#   application-controller  reconcile loop (CPU) ...... shard by cluster
#   repo-server            git clone + render (CPU) ... replicate + cache
#   redis                  cache + locks .............. HA mode
#   dex                    SSO ....................... replicate
#
# Tuning at scale:
#   - webhook refresh (not 3m poll)  ->  less repo-server load
#   - --shard N (controller replicas) ->  cluster-sharded reconcile
#   - monitor: workqueue depth, refresh latency, OOMKills
example.walkthrough: The component map (what each does, what scales, what breaks) with the controller's loop and the repo-server's CPU bottleneck — the scaling guide as architecture. The webhook-over-polling and sharding tunables are the production levers. The 'small distributed system' framing sets the engineering bar.

pitfalls: Monolith thinking: one ArgoCD deployment for 500 apps on defaults — the components scale independently; use that.
Polling at scale: 3m refresh × 500 apps × Helm renders — webhook triggers or the repo-server melts.
Unmonitored workqueue: the controller's backlog is the leading indicator — dashboard the workqueue depth.
lessons.try_it: Map a production ArgoCD: component replicas, resource requests, refresh mode (poll/webhook), sharding. Write the 1-page architecture assessment.

lessons.title: Sync Waves & Hooks in Practice
concepts: Sync waves order the chaos: `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-5"` (namespaces, CRDs) → `"0"` (the bulk) → `"5"` (the app that needs the CRDs). Waves are the DAG within a sync — lower numbers first, failures halt the wave (and the sync). The wave annotation is the deployment ordering, declared per resource.

Hooks run Jobs at sync lifecycle points: PreSync (migrations BEFORE the new version — the existing scenario's pattern, formalized), Sync (run with the sync), PostSync (smoke tests AFTER), SyncFail (cleanup/diagnostics on failure). `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded` cleans up — hooks are Jobs, and Jobs accumulate without the policy.

The hook patterns: the migration Job (PreSync, with the backoff limit and activeDeadlineSeconds — a hung migration must fail loudly, not hang the sync forever), the smoke-test Job (PostSync, failing the sync on bad health — the deployment gate), the Slack-notify Job (SyncFail — the incident signal). Each hook is a Kubernetes Job with ArgoCD annotations — standard primitives, orchestrated.

Wave/hook failure modes: the wave that never completes (a Job without a deadline — the sync hangs; always set activeDeadlineSeconds), the hook that runs twice (retry semantics — hooks must be idempotent), the PreSync migration against the OLD schema (ordering the migration vs the app correctly — the migration runs before the new code, against the old code's compatibility window).

example.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
    argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy: HookSucceeded
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 300   # hung migrations fail LOUDLY
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: acme/app:1.2.4   # the NEW version's migration...
          command: ["./migrate", "up"]
          # ...must be compatible with the OLD running code!
          # (expand-then-contract: migration adds, doesn't remove)
example.walkthrough: The PreSync migration hook: runs before the sync, cleaned up on success, deadlined at 300s (hung migrations fail loudly instead of hanging the sync). The critical comment — the new version's migration must be compatible with the OLD running code — is the expand-then-contract discipline: migrations add (columns, tables), never remove, until the old code is gone. The hook-delete-policy prevents Job accumulation.

pitfalls: Deadline-less hooks: the Job without activeDeadlineSeconds — the sync hangs forever on a stuck migration.
Contract-breaking migrations: the migration that drops the column the old code still reads — expand-then-contract, always.
Hook accumulation: no delete-policy — hundreds of completed Jobs pile up; HookSucceeded cleans.
lessons.try_it: Write a PreSync migration Job (with deadline + delete policy) and a PostSync smoke-test Job. Sync an app and observe the hook ordering in the ArgoCD UI.

lessons.title: AppProject Design for Teams
concepts: The project as a product: each team's AppProject is their platform contract — the repos they can deploy from, the namespaces they can target, the resource types allowed. Design it WITH the team (their repo layout, their namespace conventions), not FOR them — the project that fights the team's workflow gets bypassed.

The standard scopes: sourceRepos (their gitops repo + shared charts repo), destinations (their namespaces, pattern-matched: `team-a-*`), clusterResourceWhitelist (Namespace only — the escape hatch closed), namespaceResourceWhitelist (the kinds they may manage — no Roles that grant more than the project allows).

The onboarding flow: new team → platform team creates the AppProject + RBAC role + namespace + repo scaffold (the golden path: sample Application, the CI checks, the docs link) → team deploys their first app in a day. The onboarding time is the platform's UX metric — measure it, minimize it.

The guardrail evolution: start permissive (whitelists broad, learn the team's needs), tighten deliberately (the audit of what's actually used → narrow the lists), and never tighten silently (the announced change with the migration path). Guardrails are a dialogue, not a decree — the teams that trust the platform use it.

example.code:
# The team onboarding bundle (platform team's product)
#
#   1. AppProject: team-a
#        sources: [github.com/acme/team-a-gitops, charts-shared]
#        destinations: [{server: prod, namespace: team-a-*}]
#        cluster whitelist: [Namespace]  (no escape hatch)
#   2. RBAC: role:team-a -> (IdP group team-a) : sync/get on team-a/*
#   3. Namespace: team-a-prod (with ResourceQuota + NetworkPolicy)
#   4. Repo scaffold: sample Application + CI (conftest) + README
#   5. Docs: 'your first deploy in 30 minutes'
#
# Metric: time from 'we want GitOps' to first production deploy.
example.walkthrough: The onboarding bundle (project + RBAC + namespace + scaffold + docs) as the platform team's product, with the onboarding time as the UX metric. The guardrail evolution (permissive → tighten deliberately → never silently) treats platform-team relationship as dialogue. The 'designed WITH not FOR' principle prevents the bypassed-platform failure.

pitfalls: Decree guardrails: the project designed without the team — bypassed within a month; co-design it.
Silent tightening: the whitelist narrowed without warning — the deploy that worked Friday fails Monday; announce + migrate.
No onboarding metric: the platform nobody measures — time-to-first-deploy is the UX that matters.
lessons.try_it: Design the full onboarding bundle for a fictional team (project YAML, RBAC entries, namespace, scaffold README). Time a dry-run: how long to first deploy?

lessons.title: Backup, Restore & Recovery Drills
concepts: What needs backing up: the git repos (the desired state — already distributed, the primary backup), ArgoCD's own config (the root apps, projects, RBAC — IN GIT, the 'GitOps managing GitOps' rule), and the cluster state ArgoCD doesn't own (its CRDs' live state, Redis — Velero for the argocd namespace). The recovery equation: git + Velero + the runbook = rebuilt control plane.

The prune-disaster scenario: an over-broad prune deletes a namespace (the existing 'Fifty Apps, One Cluster' energy). Recovery: the resources are all in git — re-sync restores them (the manifests, not the data). The DATA needs its own story (Velero/Restic for PVs — GitOps restores the shape, not the contents).

The recovery drill (quarterly): pick a non-prod cluster, delete the ArgoCD installation (or a workload namespace), rebuild from git + Velero, time it, document the gaps. The drill's output is the runbook update — every drill finds something (the missing sealed-secret key, the unrecorded cluster registration).

The RTO/RPO framing: RTO (how fast the control plane rebuilds — measured by the drill), RPO (how much git history could be lost — ~zero, it's distributed; how much cluster-live state — the Velero schedule). The numbers go in the platform's SLA doc — the recovery story auditors and incident commanders actually read.

example.code:
# The recovery equation
#
#   git repos (desired state, distributed)   = primary backup
#   + ArgoCD config IN GIT (root apps, projects, RBAC)
#   + Velero (argocd namespace, PVs)        = cluster-live state
#   + runbook (practiced quarterly)         = the how
#   = rebuilt control plane in <RTO>
#
# Prune disaster: re-sync restores SHAPE (manifests in git).
#   DATA needs its own restore (Velero/Restic) -- shape != contents.
# Drill: delete non-prod ArgoCD -> rebuild -> time it -> update runbook.
example.walkthrough: The recovery equation (git + Velero + runbook = rebuilt control plane) with the shape-vs-contents distinction (re-sync restores manifests, not PV data) and the quarterly drill as the runbook's maintenance. The RTO/RPO framing gives the SLA language. The 'GitOps managing GitOps' rule (ArgoCD's config in git) is the prevention for the lost-control-plane incident.

pitfalls: Shape/data confusion: re-sync restores manifests — the database needs Velero/Restic; drill both.
Undrilled runbook: the recovery doc nobody's run — quarterly drills or it's fiction.
ArgoCD config outside git: the root apps on a laptop — the control plane gets GitOps discipline too.
lessons.try_it: Run the drill on a test cluster: back up (Velero), delete the ArgoCD namespace, rebuild from git + backup, time the recovery, and update the runbook with the gaps found.

lessons.title: Welcome: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp builds the complete GitOps-with-Terraform-and-Kubernetes skill set: the Terraform language and state mastery, modules and collaboration, ArgoCD and Flux GitOps, policy as code, Ansible integration, and immutable image pipelines. Two loops run through everything: Terraform's plan/apply loop (the infrastructure converging) and the GitOps reconciliation loop (the cluster converging) — learn to see both, always.

How to work it: study the domains in order (each layer assumes the last — the language before the state, ArgoCD before the projects), do the try-it exercises against real tooling (kind/k3d clusters, local Terraform, the free TFC tier — this subject is learned by doing), keep a lab journal (every error and its fix — the journal becomes your runbook), and finish with the capstone platform build.

The stance: operator's mindset — every concept gets the 'what breaks at 3 AM?' test, every tool gets the 'what's the blast radius?' question, every pattern gets the 'how do I recover?' drill. This bootcamp trains the engineer who gets paged, not just the one who passes interviews — though you'll do that too.

What you'll have: Terraform fluency (language, state, modules), GitOps operations (ArgoCD + Flux, projects, image automation), guardrails (policy as code, admission control), the Ansible handoff, image pipelines — and the capstone: a production-grade GitOps platform you built, documented, and can demo.

  ORDER: language -> state -> modules -> cloud -> ArgoCD ->

     (each layer assumes the last)

example.walkthrough: The welcome orients with the two-loops mental model (plan/apply + reconcile — see both always), the ordered path, the real-tooling method, and the operator's mindset (3 AM test, blast radius, recovery). The outcome inventory sets the bar: fluency plus a demoable platform.

pitfalls: Tutorial-only learning: this subject is learned by doing — the try-its need real clusters and real applies.
Skipping the journal: the lab journal becomes the runbook — errors documented are errors halved.
Interview-only mindset: the 3 AM test — train for the page, not just the interview.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: The Two Loops
concepts: Loop one — Terraform: write → fmt/validate → plan → review → apply → state. The discipline is the review (the plan is the diff that matters — read it like code review) and the state hygiene (remote, locked, backed up). Every Terraform incident in this bootcamp traces to skipping a loop step — usually the plan review.

Loop two — GitOps: commit → PR → checks (plan/policy) → merge → reconcile → observe. The discipline is the git discipline (small commits, reviewed PRs, meaningful messages — the git log is the audit trail) and the reconciliation trust (the agent converges; don't kubectl around it). Every GitOps incident traces to breaking the loop — usually the manual edit.

The loops interact: Terraform provisions the platform (the cluster, the registries, ArgoCD itself — via the cloud/CI loop), GitOps runs the workloads (the apps, the policies — via the reconcile loop). The platform team lives in both loops; the app teams live mostly in the GitOps loop. Know which loop you're in.

The study rhythm: one domain per study block, try-it in the lab, journal the errors, and the weekly review (re-read the journal — the patterns compound). The two loops are also the learning loops: theory → practice → error → runbook. The journal is the state file of your learning — don't lose it.

example.code:
THE TWO LOOPS (study + operations)
  TERRAFORM: write -> fmt/validate -> plan -> REVIEW -> apply
     -> state. (Incidents = skipped steps, usually plan review.)
  GITOPS: commit -> PR -> checks -> merge -> reconcile ->
     observe. (Incidents = broken loop, usually manual edits.)
  INTERACTION: Terraform provisions the PLATFORM (cluster,
     ArgoCD itself); GitOps runs the WORKLOADS (apps, policies).
     Platform team: both loops. App teams: mostly GitOps.
  STUDY: domain per block -> try-it -> journal errors ->
     weekly review. The journal is your learning's state file.
example.walkthrough: The two-loops strategy gives the operational rhythm (each loop's discipline and characteristic incident) plus the interaction model (Terraform provisions platform, GitOps runs workloads) and the study rhythm mapping onto the loops. The journal-as-state-file metaphor ties the method together.

pitfalls: Skipping plan review: the Terraform incident generator — the plan is the diff; read it.
kubectl around the agent: the GitOps incident generator — trust the reconciliation; fix in git.
Loop confusion: applying platform changes via GitOps or workload changes via Terraform — know which loop.
lessons.try_it: Write 200 words: which loop will dominate your daily work, and what discipline will you enforce on yourself for it?

lessons.title: Course Map: From HCL to Fleet GitOps
concepts: The path: Terraform Language (write it) → State (understand the memory) → Modules (scale the authoring) → Terraform Cloud (collaborate) → ArgoCD (the GitOps engine) → Flux (the alternative engine) → Policy as Code (the guardrails) → Ansible (the configuration complement) → Packer (the immutable artifacts) → Capstone (the platform). Nine domains, one platform.

The existing content slots in: the original GitOps domain (core concepts — the principles this bootcamp's expand deepens), the ArgoCD domain (first contact — the mastery domain deepens), and the scenarios (the incident catalog — referenced throughout as the 'existing scenarios'). The rebuild preserves and extends — the map shows where.

The pacing: Terraform first (domains 1-4, the foundation — don't touch ArgoCD until state makes sense), then the GitOps engines (5-6, the core — ArgoCD deeply, Flux comparatively), then the platform disciplines (7-9, the guardrails and complements), then the capstone (the synthesis). Roughly: foundation 40%, engines 30%, disciplines 20%, capstone 10%.

The checkpoints: after Terraform Cloud, you can collaborate on IaC safely; after ArgoCD, you can run GitOps for a team; after Policy, you can gate it; after the capstone, you can platform it. Each checkpoint is a job-ready skill — the map is also the resume.

pitfalls: ArgoCD before state: the engines assume the foundation — state confusion poisons GitOps understanding.
Engines as rivals: ArgoCD deeply, Flux comparatively — the goal is judgment, not tribalism.
Skipping to capstone: the synthesis assumes the disciplines — the platform without guardrails is the incident.

lessons.title: Interview & Exam Strategy
concepts: The interview themes: the two loops (explain plan/apply AND reconcile — the full picture), state (the most-asked topic: 'what is state? locking? drift?'), the ArgoCD/Flux comparison (judgment, not tribalism), policy as code (the senior signal), and the incident stories (every scenario in this bootcamp is an interview answer — 'tell me about a time' with the mechanism and the fix).

The answer structure: mechanism → incident → fix → principle. ('State locking: the DynamoDB mutex prevents concurrent-apply corruption — we had two engineers corrupt a Monday state — now S3+DynamoDB everywhere — the principle: the state is the crown jewels.') The bootcamp's scenarios are pre-built in this structure — rehearse them aloud.

The hands-on proof: interviewers trust the lab journal and the capstone over claims — 'here's my GitOps platform, here's the repo, here's the demo' beats 'I'm proficient in ArgoCD.' The capstone is the portfolio piece; the journal is the depth proof. Build both as if the interview is the audience.

The senior differentiators: blast-radius thinking (every answer includes 'and the failure mode is...'), the credential math (push vs pull), policy rollout discipline (advisory before mandatory), and the honest limits (what GitOps doesn't solve — the data layer, the SaaS APIs). Seniors name the failure modes; juniors name the tools.

example.code:
INTERVIEW & EXAM STRATEGY
  THEMES: two loops; STATE (most-asked); ArgoCD/Flux judgment;
     policy as code (senior signal); incident stories.
  ANSWER STRUCTURE: mechanism -> incident -> fix -> principle.
     (The scenarios are pre-built this way -- rehearse aloud.)
  PROOF: the capstone repo + demo beats claims; the journal
     proves depth. Build for the interview as audience.
  SENIOR SIGNALS: blast-radius thinking; credential math;
     rollout discipline; honest limits (data layer, SaaS APIs).
     Seniors name failure modes; juniors name tools.
example.walkthrough: The interview strategy gives the theme list, the mechanism→incident→fix→principle answer structure (with the worked example), the proof-over-claims guidance (capstone + journal as portfolio), and the senior differentiators (failure modes, credential math, rollout discipline, honest limits). The seniors-name-failures line is the positioning advice.

pitfalls: Tool-listing: 'I know Terraform, ArgoCD, Flux' — the interview wants mechanisms and failure modes, not nouns.
Unexamined claims: every 'proficient' needs the repo + demo — proof, not adjectives.
Junior framing: answering without the blast radius — add 'and the failure mode is...' to everything.
lessons.try_it: Rehearse aloud: pick three scenarios from the bootcamp and deliver each as mechanism → incident → fix → principle (2 minutes each). Record yourself.

lessons.title: Architecture: The Platform Blueprint
concepts: The blueprint: Terraform provisions the platform (VPC, EKS/cluster, ECR/registry, ArgoCD via Helm — the platform layer, in the cloud loop), GitOps runs the workloads (the app-of-apps root, team AppProjects, the policy bundle — in the reconcile loop). The two loops, one platform — the bootcamp's thesis, architected.

The component map: foundation (network, IAM, state backends — Terraform), the cluster (EKS + node groups + addons — Terraform), the GitOps engine (ArgoCD + projects + RBAC — Terraform-deployed, git-configured), the guardrails (Kyverno policies + Conftest in CI — git-deployed), the workloads (3 sample apps via ApplicationSet — git-deployed), the images (Packer pipeline or registry automation — the artifact loop).

The tenancy design: platform team's project (full privilege, the engine itself), team-a/team-b projects (scoped — the multi-tenancy lesson applied), the policy bundle (the non-negotiables: no latest, required labels, encrypted S3 — the policy lessons applied), and the onboarding bundle (the new-team scaffold — the platform as product).

The operational design: monitoring (reconciliation health, drift alerts — the observability lessons), backup (Velero + git — the recovery lesson), the runbooks (the incident scenarios, rehearsed), and the SLOs (commit-to-converged latency, the GitOps metric). The blueprint includes the operating, not just the building.

example.code:
CAPSTONE BLUEPRINT
  TERRAFORM (platform loop): VPC, EKS, registry, ArgoCD-Helm,
     state backends, IAM.
  GITOPS (reconcile loop): app-of-apps root, team projects,
     policy bundle, 3 sample apps (ApplicationSet).
  TENANCY: platform project (full) + team-a/b (scoped) +
     policy bundle (non-negotiables) + onboarding scaffold.
  OPERATIONS: reconciliation monitoring, drift alerts,
     Velero + git backup, incident runbooks, SLOs.
  The blueprint includes the OPERATING, not just the building.
example.walkthrough: The blueprint assembles every domain into one architecture: Terraform's platform loop, GitOps' workload loop, the tenancy design, the policy bundle, and the operational layer (monitoring, backup, runbooks, SLOs). The 'operating not just building' principle makes it production-grade rather than demo-grade.

pitfalls: Building without operating: the platform without monitoring/backup/runbooks/SLOs is a demo, not production.
Single-loop design: Terraform-only or GitOps-only — the capstone requires both loops, each in its layer.
Tenancy as afterthought: the projects and guardrails are architecture, not polish — design them in.
lessons.try_it: Draw the full blueprint (one page): components, loops, tenancy, guardrails, operations. Review it against the domain lessons — what's missing?

lessons.title: Build Guide: Assembling the Platform
concepts: The build sequence: (1) foundation — Terraform the network, state backends, IAM (the state lessons applied); (2) cluster — EKS via Terraform (the modules lesson — or the registry's EKS module, adapted); (3) engine — ArgoCD via Terraform Helm release + the root app-of-apps in git (the bootstrap); (4) tenancy — projects, RBAC, namespaces (the projects lesson); (5) guardrails — Kyverno bundle + Conftest CI (the policy lessons); (6) workloads — 3 apps via ApplicationSet + image automation; (7) operations — monitoring, Velero, runbooks.

The git layout: platform repo (Terraform — the cloud loop) + gitops repo (workloads, projects, policies — the reconcile loop) + app repos (the sample services). Three repos, two loops, one platform — the layout IS the architecture. Branch protection + CODEOWNERS on all three (the review discipline).

The verification gates: after each phase, the checkpoint (foundation: `terraform plan` clean + state remote; engine: ArgoCD healthy + root app synced; tenancy: team-b can't touch team-a; guardrails: the `:latest` deploy blocked; workloads: the image automation loop traced end-to-end; operations: the game-day drill passed). Gates, not hopes.

The journal requirement: every error, every fix, every workaround — the build journal becomes the operations runbook's first draft. The capstone's second deliverable (after the platform) is the journal-turned-runbook — the proof of operator thinking.

example.code:
BUILD SEQUENCE (gates, not hopes)
  1. FOUNDATION: Terraform network/IAM/state (plan clean, remote)
  2. CLUSTER: EKS via Terraform (modules lesson applied)
  3. ENGINE: ArgoCD Helm + root app-of-apps (bootstrap)
  4. TENANCY: projects, RBAC, namespaces (isolation verified)
  5. GUARDRAILS: Kyverno + Conftest (latest blocked)
  6. WORKLOADS: 3 apps, ApplicationSet, image automation (loop traced)
  7. OPERATIONS: monitoring, Velero, runbooks (game-day passed)
  REPOS: platform (Terraform) + gitops (workloads) + apps.
     Three repos, two loops -- the layout IS the architecture.
  SECOND DELIVERABLE: the journal-turned-runbook.
example.walkthrough: The build guide sequences the seven phases with verification gates after each (not hopes — checks), gives the three-repo layout (layout as architecture), and mandates the journal-turned-runbook as the second deliverable. The gates make the build verifiable at every step.

pitfalls: Gateless building: phase 7 on a broken phase 2 — the checkpoints exist to catch it early; honor them.
Monorepo muddle: platform Terraform and workload manifests in one undifferentiated repo — the loops need their repos.
Journal-less building: the errors unrecorded — the runbook's first draft is the build journal; keep it.
lessons.try_it: Execute phases 1-3 this week (foundation → cluster → engine). Journal every error. Verify each gate before proceeding.

lessons.title: Demo & Handoff: Proving It Works
concepts: The demo script (15 minutes): (1) the commit — push a change, show the PR checks (plan + policy); (2) the merge — watch ArgoCD sync (the loop, live); (3) the guardrail — attempt the `:latest` deploy, watch Kyverno block it; (4) the tenancy — team-b's sync attempt on team-a's namespace, denied; (5) the recovery — delete a workload namespace, watch the re-sync restore it; (6) the image loop — push a patch tag, trace registry → git → cluster.

The handoff package: the blueprint doc, the three repos (with READMEs — the 'how to run this' for each loop), the runbook (the journal distilled — the incident scenarios with the platform-specific steps), the SLO dashboard (commit-to-converged latency, reconciliation health), and the recorded demo (the artifact that outlives the presentation).

The narrative: 'I built the platform teams use to ship safely' — the demo tells the story (the guardrails catching the bad deploy, the tenancy holding, the recovery working), the repos prove the depth, the runbook proves the operator thinking. The capstone is the interview portfolio piece — narrate it as the platform engineer you are.

The retrospective: what broke, what you'd change, what you'd add next (multi-cluster fleet, the Flux migration path, the cost-optimization layer) — the honest engineering review. The retrospective is the senior signal: juniors present successes; seniors present the failures and the next iteration.

example.code:
DEMO SCRIPT (15 min)
  1. COMMIT: push -> PR checks (plan + policy) shown
  2. MERGE: ArgoCD syncs live (the loop, observed)
  3. GUARDRAIL: :latest deploy attempted -> Kyverno BLOCKS
  4. TENANCY: team-b -> team-a namespace: DENIED
  5. RECOVERY: delete workload ns -> re-sync RESTORES
  6. IMAGE LOOP: patch tag -> registry -> git -> cluster (traced)
  HANDOFF: blueprint + 3 repos (READMEs) + runbook +
     SLO dashboard + recorded demo.
  NARRATIVE: 'the platform teams use to ship safely.'
  RETROSPECTIVE: what broke, what changes, what's next.
     (Seniors present failures + next iteration.)
example.walkthrough: The demo script (six beats, each proving a bootcamp lesson live), the handoff package (blueprint, repos, runbook, SLOs, recording), the narrative framing, and the retrospective as the senior signal. The demo is designed as the interview portfolio piece — every beat maps to a domain.

pitfalls: Feature tour demo: clicking through the UI — the demo proves PROPERTIES (guardrails hold, recovery works), not features.
No handoff: the live demo without the repos/runbook — the artifacts outlive the presentation; package them.
Success-only retrospective: the failures and next iterations are the senior signal — present them.
lessons.try_it: Record your 15-minute demo following the script. Then write the 1-page retrospective: what broke, what changes, what's next.

Replace the in-repo Secret manifest with an ExternalSecret referencing the Vault path.

Run terraform fmt -check -recursive; fix all formatting.
Run terraform validate; fix all errors.
Set up pre-commit with fmt + validate hooks.

Remove the middle user from the list; plan and observe the cascade (addresses [2..4] all recreate).
Convert to for_each over a set; plan the same removal and observe only one destroy.
Write 200 words: the identity rule (count for fungible, for_each for named).

The cascade shows as 'forces replacement' on the renumbered instances.
toset() converts the list; each.value is the stable key.

labs.title: State Backend Migration Lab
labs.objective: Migrate local state to a versioned, encrypted, locked S3 backend.

Apply a trivial config locally first (local state).
Add the backend block; run terraform init -migrate-state.
Verify: state list works, bucket shows the key, versions accumulate.
Simulate a stale lock (kill -9 a sleep-wrapped apply is overkill — use force-unlock on a test lock) and practice safe unlock.

checks.hint: -migrate-state copies local to remote; answer 'yes' to the prompt.
Check the bucket versioning shows multiple versions after two applies.
force-unlock needs the exact lock ID from the error — copy it precisely.

labs.title: Drift Detection Pipeline Lab
labs.objective: Build the nightly drift-detection CI job with triage.
steps: Write the CI job: init, plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode, alert on exit 2.
Introduce manual drift (console tag change); watch the job detect it (exit 2).
Triage path A: codify (import + config) for a legitimate change.
Triage path B: reconverge (apply) for an illegitimate change.
Document your team's triage decision tree (codify vs reconverge criteria).

checks.hint: -detailed-exitcode is the sensor: 0 clean, 1 error, 2 drift.
The triage decision: 'should the world match config, or config match world?'
Schedule it nightly; drift detected in the morning is drift half-fixed.

labs.success_message: A working drift pipeline with both triage paths exercised and documented.

labs.title: Module Authoring Lab

Tag v1.0.0; call via git ?ref= from a root config.
Release v1.1.0 (new optional variable); verify the caller still plans clean.
Write the CHANGELOG entries for both releases.

?ref=v1.0.0 pins; test the v1.1.0 bump as a separate step.
CHANGELOG: breaking vs feature vs fix — practice the semver language.

labs.success_message: A published, versioned, example-tested module with a changelog.

Write the runbook entry: 'my app won't sync' (the debug sequence).

Write the ApplicationSet (Git generator over apps/*); apply it.
Verify 3 Applications appear and sync.
Add a 4th directory; watch the Application generate automatically.
Rename a template field; verify all 4 update from the single template.

Attempt: team-a Application with a ClusterRole → observe the denial.
Document the isolation matrix (who can do what, where) as the 1-page proof.

The minor-tag non-promotion proves the gate — check the policy events.
Lag = registry scan + git push + source refresh + reconcile; measure each.

labs.success_message: A traced, timed image loop with the deliberate gate proven (patch yes, minor no).

labs.title: Flux Bootstrap Lab

Compare with your ArgoCD lab: write 300 words on the architectural differences you felt.

flux get kustomizations is the status view; flux logs --level=error the debug.

Document the rollout metrics at each rung (the ladder, evidenced).

simulations.title: Drift nobody committed
simulations.brief: The GitOps agent reports the payments namespace as 'OutOfSync' — but git is clean and nobody merged today. Someone changed the cluster by hand. Work the drift.

steps.symptom: ArgoCD-style status: payments app OutOfSync. Git log: no merges in 48 hours.
evidence: App: payments. Sync: OutOfSync. Diff: Deployment/payments-api replicas 3 (git) vs 5 (live).
kubectl scale deployment/payments-api --replicas=5 by on-call, 14:12, 'to handle the sale'.
options: The drift is a manual scale — reconcile by updating the git manifest to the intended replica count, not by clicking sync blindly
Click 'Sync' immediately to force the cluster back to 3
Delete the app and let GitOps recreate it
The drift will resolve itself on the next sync cycle
steps.explain: Reconciliation is observe-diff-sync: the diff tells you a human scaled for a real reason (the sale). Update git to declare the intended state — syncing blindly would undo a deliberate, load-driven change and re-create the incident.

steps.symptom: The sale ends tonight. The replica count should return to 3 tomorrow.
evidence: Post-sale: scale back to 3. Owner: on-call. Method: currently 'remember to do it'.
payments-api replicas in git: still 3 (never updated for the sale).
options: Make the temporary change explicit in git (or a scheduled override) with a revert plan — 'remember to do it' is how drift becomes permanent
Leave it at 5 — extra capacity is harmless
Scale it back by hand tomorrow and tell no one
Delete the deployment and recreate it at 3
steps.explain: Git is the single source of truth, including for temporary changes: declare the override in git with its expiry, or schedule the revert. Manual changes with memory-based follow-through are exactly how OutOfSync becomes the permanent state.

steps.symptom: Leadership asks how to stop hand-edits to the cluster entirely.
evidence: 47 engineers hold cluster-admin. 'Everyone needs it for emergencies.'
No policy blocks manual mutation of GitOps-managed namespaces.
options: Remove standing cluster-admin, scope emergency access with expiry, and let the GitOps agent own managed namespaces
Keep cluster-admin for everyone — emergencies need speed
Add a wiki page asking people not to hand-edit
Move the GitOps agent to a different cluster
steps.explain: Pull-based GitOps plus scoped RBAC is the structural fix: the in-cluster agent reconciles, humans propose changes via git, and emergency access is temporary and audited. Forty-seven permanent cluster-admins is not an emergency plan — it's the drift factory.

simulations.debrief: Drift is detected automatically by the reconcile loop — but resolved deliberately: understand why the live state diverged, declare the intended state in git, and remove the standing access that lets drift happen.

simulations.title: The mutable latest tag
simulations.brief: Two clusters run 'the same' manifest from git, but behave differently. Both deploy image api:latest. The tag moved between their sync times. Fix the reference.

steps.symptom: Staging and prod both sync api:latest from the same commit — but run different code.
evidence: api:latest resolved at sync: sha256:aaa1 (built Monday).
api:latest resolved at sync: sha256:bbb2 (built Wednesday). Same git commit.
options: Pin immutable references — digests or version tags — so the manifest describes exactly what each cluster runs
Sync both clusters at the same time so latest resolves identically
This is fine — latest is always the newest code
Stop using staging — it causes confusion
steps.explain: With mutable tags like 'latest', the repo stops describing what's actually running — two syncs of the same commit resolve to different artifacts. Immutable references make the manifest a true statement about the cluster.

steps.symptom: The team pins versions but CI still pushes api:2.4.1 twice — the second build overwrote the first.
evidence: api:2.4.1 pushed Monday (sha256:aaa1), pushed again Wednesday (sha256:bbb2). Tag reassigned.
Rollback to '2.4.1' restored Wednesday's code, not Monday's.
options: Make tags immutable in the registry (or deploy by digest) — a version tag must name one artifact forever
Version tags are just labels — overwriting is normal
Never roll back — always roll forward
Use timestamps in tags so they never collide
steps.explain: A version tag that gets reassigned is a mutable tag wearing a version costume — rollback to '2.4.1' must mean Monday's artifact, deterministically. Immutable tags or digest references make the version a promise, not a suggestion.

steps.symptom: GitOps is configured with auto-sync, and a bad image just auto-deployed to production.
evidence: Automated sync: enabled, prune: true. No health gates.
Bad image (crash loop) synced to prod at 03:12. Auto-sync faithfully deployed the declared state.
options: The declared state was wrong, not the sync: gate what gets declared (CI promotion, image verification) — auto-sync only deploys what's in git
Disable auto-sync — manual sync is safer
Auto-sync is broken — replace the GitOps tool
The bad image is CI's fault, not GitOps' — no action needed
steps.explain: Auto-sync deploys the declared state faithfully — that's its job. The control point is what gets declared: CI promotion gates, image verification, and progressive delivery decide which artifact git may reference. Blaming the sync loop misses the actual gate.

simulations.debrief: Immutable image references keep git honest: digests or pinned version tags, registry immutability, and promotion gates controlling what git may declare. The manifest must be a true statement about the cluster.

simulations.title: Secret committed to git
simulations.brief: The GitOps repo contains a base64'd database password in a manifest. 'It's encoded, not encrypted,' the audit notes. The whole repo is cloned to every engineer's laptop. Fix the secret handling.

steps.symptom: Secret manifest in git: password stored base64-encoded. 40+ clones of the repo exist.
options: Rotate the password immediately, then replace the manifest with a reference resolved at runtime from a secrets manager
It's base64 — that's basically encrypted. Leave it.
Delete the manifest from git history — the clones don't matter
Restrict who can clone the repo
steps.explain: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — every clone holder can decode it in one command. Secrets don't belong in git in any form: rotate now, then store references (ExternalSecrets, Vault Agent) and let the cluster resolve real values at runtime.

steps.symptom: The team proposes SealedSecrets-style encryption: encrypted values committed, decrypted in-cluster.
evidence: 'We encrypt with the cluster key and commit the ciphertext. Git stays the source of truth.'
Key rotation story: unclear. Multi-cluster story: unclear. Audit of who decrypted what: none.
options: Encrypted-in-git is acceptable only with a real key-management and rotation story; otherwise prefer manager references resolved at runtime
Encrypted in git is always wrong — never do it
Encrypted in git is always fine — encryption solves everything
Just use base64 — simpler
steps.explain: Encrypted secrets in git can work, but the security moves to key management: rotation, scope, audit, multi-cluster. Without answers there, it's obfuscation with extra steps. Manager references keep the secret out of git entirely — the simpler invariant to defend.

steps.symptom: CI needs cloud credentials to run Terraform — currently a long-lived key in CI variables.
evidence: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: AKIA... (created 2023, never rotated). Scope: admin.
The GitOps agent runs in-cluster with its own scoped service account.
options: Move to pull-based delivery and short-lived workload identity — CI never holds cluster or cloud credentials
Rotate the CI key yearly — that's sufficient
Scope the key down but keep it long-lived
Put the key in the GitOps repo so it's versioned
steps.explain: Pull-based delivery beats push-based precisely here: the in-cluster agent pulls changes, so CI never needs cluster credentials — a major reduction in secret sprawl. Pair with short-lived workload identity and the 2023 admin key retires permanently.

simulations.debrief: Secrets don't belong in git — encoded, encrypted, or otherwise. Store references, resolve at runtime from a manager, and let pull-based delivery eliminate the credentials CI used to need.

simulations.title: CI holds the cluster keys
simulations.brief: The deploy pipeline pushes to the cluster with a kubeconfig stored in CI variables. The kubeconfig is cluster-admin, 2 years old, and shared across 5 pipelines. Redesign the delivery.

steps.symptom: CI pushes manifests with a 2-year-old cluster-admin kubeconfig shared by 5 pipelines.
evidence: Age: 2 years. Scope: cluster-admin. Shared across: 5 pipelines, 3 teams.
Any of the 5 pipelines can delete any namespace. No audit per pipeline.
options: Switch to pull-based GitOps: the in-cluster agent syncs from git; CI only commits manifests and never touches the cluster
Rotate the kubeconfig — a fresh cluster-admin key fixes it
Give each pipeline its own cluster-admin kubeconfig
Shorten the key's name so it's harder to guess
steps.explain: Pull-based delivery removes the entire credential class: CI writes to git, the agent inside the cluster pulls. No kubeconfig in CI means no 2-year-old cluster-admin key to rotate, scope, or leak — the secret sprawl disappears structurally.

steps.symptom: One pipeline still needs to run database migrations — it genuinely must reach the cluster.
evidence: Job: run migrations pre-deploy. Needs: db access, not cluster-admin.
Today it uses the shared cluster-admin kubeconfig 'because it's there'.
options: Give the migration job its own scoped, short-lived credential limited to what migrations need
Keep using the shared kubeconfig — migrations are trusted
Run migrations by hand from a laptop instead
Skip migrations — the app handles schema drift
steps.explain: The exception proves the pattern: the one job that must reach the cluster gets its own scoped, short-lived credential — not the shared skeleton key. Least privilege applies to automation exactly as it does to humans.

steps.symptom: After the migration to pull-based, deploys feel slower — 'push was instant.'
evidence: Push deploy: 40s. GitOps sync interval: 3min poll. 'It feels broken.'
Webhook from git host to the agent: not configured.
options: Configure the git webhook so pushes trigger near-instant syncs — pull-based with webhooks is as fast as push
Go back to push — speed matters more than security
Reduce the poll interval to 5 seconds
Deploys don't need to be fast
steps.explain: Pull-based doesn't mean slow: a webhook from the git host notifies the agent on push, giving push-like speed with pull-based security. The 3-minute poll is the default, not the design — wire the webhook.

simulations.debrief: Pull-based delivery: the agent inside the cluster pulls from git, CI never holds cluster credentials, and webhooks keep it fast. Exceptions get scoped, short-lived credentials — never the shared skeleton key.

simulations.title: One giant app-of-apps
simulations.brief: The platform team manages all 60 services with a single GitOps application. Every sync touches everything, one team's bad commit blocks all deploys, and nobody can tell who owns what. Decompose it.

steps.symptom: Single GitOps app, 60 services, one sync scope. A bad commit in team A's manifests blocks team B's urgent deploy.
evidence: Applications: 1 ('everything'). Sources: 1 repo, 60 service dirs. Sync failures: block all 60.
Team B's hotfix waited 6 hours for team A's broken manifest to be reverted.
options: Decompose into app-of-apps: a parent app per team/scope, each with its own sync policy and blast radius
Keep one app — the coupling encourages careful commits
Split into 60 separate GitOps installations
Let team B edit team A's manifests to unblock themselves
steps.explain: The app-of-apps pattern composes Applications hierarchically: each team gets its own sync scope, policies, and blast radius under a parent. One giant sync couples 60 teams' fates; hierarchy decouples them while keeping one pane of glass.

steps.symptom: After decomposition, team C's app syncs fine but its service can't reach team D's database.
evidence: NetworkPolicies: none. 'The old monolith app handled networking implicitly.'
Team C: 'It worked when everything was one app!'
options: The decomposition surfaced implicit coupling — define the cross-team contract explicitly (service endpoints, network policy, ownership)
Merge C and D back into one app
Give every app cluster-wide network access
It worked before, so the decomposition is wrong
steps.explain: Decomposition surfaces hidden coupling — that's a feature. The old giant app masked cross-team dependencies; now they become explicit contracts: endpoints, policies, owners. Implicit coupling that 'just worked' is tech debt with a good disguise.

steps.symptom: Each team now wants its own repo, its own sync schedule, its own tool version.
evidence: Team A: own repo. Team B: hourly sync. Team C: different GitOps version.
options: Standardize the platform contract (repo layout, sync policy, versions) and let teams vary inside it — paved road, not 60 snowflakes
Let every team do exactly what it wants — autonomy above all
Force everything identical — no variation allowed
One repo for everyone, no exceptions
steps.explain: App-of-apps gives each team its own scope — inside a platform contract. Total freedom recreates 60 snowflakes a 4-person platform team can't support; total rigidity recreates the monolith. The paved road standardizes the how and frees the what.

simulations.debrief: App-of-apps decomposes the giant sync into hierarchical scopes: each team owns its sync policy and blast radius, hidden coupling becomes explicit contracts, and the platform contract keeps 60 services supportable.

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
